**World War II Scientific Developments (Dyslexia-Accessible Version)**

World War II caused many scientific and technological changes. These changes became matters of life and death. The war itself changed how governments worked with scientists. Governments spent money on weapons and other technologies needed for the war and for national security.

In fall 1939, British scientists quickly changed their work. They moved from pure research to helping the war effort.

Advances in radio waves led to radar. Radar gave early warning of enemy attacks. Other advances added electronics like microwaves and early computers to military use. This helped spread electronics into everyday life after the war.

Allied efforts to break Nazi spy codes started the first simple computers. British mathematician Alan Turing and his team worked for the British Secret Service. They tried to break the Nazi Enigma code, which seemed unbreakable. To do this, they built a device. This device tested hundreds of thousands of possible code keys in intercepted messages. They succeeded in breaking the code.

Another computing breakthrough was ENIAC. ENIAC stood for Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer. The U.S. Army first used it to calculate artillery shots. It calculated much faster than earlier machines, using electricity instead of moving parts. By 1955, ENIAC had done more calculations than all humans combined up to that point.

Medical science also advanced during the war. A key medical development was penicillin. Scientists improved how to make and use penicillin. This allowed mass production of the antibiotic.

Charles Drew, an African American doctor, made another life-saving advance. He developed a better way to store blood plasma. Plasma could be kept longer than whole blood. It also worked well as a replacement for whole-blood transfusions in emergencies.

However, racial bias appeared in 1941. The U.S. Red Cross followed a War Department rule. They labeled blood and plasma as either "White" or "Negro." Dr. Drew resigned from the National Blood Bank because this policy was racist and unscientific.

The biggest scientific effort was building the atomic bomb. In December 1938, German physicists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann split atoms. This discovery was called nuclear fission. A few months later, Germany started a secret program, the Uranium Club, to build an atomic bomb.

German-born physicist Albert Einstein had recently moved to the U.S. He knew the danger of Nazi research. With help from physicist Leo Szilard, Einstein wrote a letter to President Roosevelt. The letter warned about Nazi work and urged the U.S. to start its own program.

By the late 1930s, British scientists and others believed an atomic bomb was possible. Teams of physicists, including refugees from Nazi Germany, began experiments. They studied nuclear chain reactions, which cause atomic explosions.

In August 1942, the U.S. government started the top-secret Manhattan Project. Workers at many sites across the U.S. began building the first atomic bomb. Sites included Los Alamos in New Mexico, Oak Ridge in Tennessee, and Hanford in Washington State. About 600,000 people worked on this urgent project.

Germany and Japan also tried to build atomic bombs. Germany faced problems. Many top German scientists had left Germany. Some even helped the Manhattan Project. Also, Hitler preferred funding V2 bombers for attacks on England over an atomic bomb.

Japan started its own project in 1941. Physicist Yoshio Nishina led it, called Ni-Go. Japan learned little from Germany due to U.S. air raids and lack of shared information. Progress on the Japanese atomic bomb was slow.

In July 1945, the Manhattan Project succeeded. Scientists detonated a test bomb at Trinity in New Mexico. William L. Laurence, the project historian, described this moment: "On that moment hung eternity. Time stood still. Space contracted to a pinpoint. It was as though the earth had opened and the skies split. One felt as though they had been privileged to witness the Birth of the World—to be present at the moment of Creation when the Lord Said: Let there be light."

President Roosevelt died suddenly in April 1945. Vice President Harry S. Truman became president. Truman then had to decide whether to use the new atomic weapon.

**Trenches on the Western Front**

The stalemate in late 1914 led to trenches. Both sides dug them deep for protection. These trenches became the main fighting area of World War I.

Constant artillery fire and deep mud made trench life hard. Soldiers dug down to hide from enemy shells. They often stayed in one spot for days.

German troops dug deeper, stronger trenches early on. They expected to stay there a long time. Allied trenches started simple but improved over the years.

At their longest, trenches stretched about 500 miles across France and Belgium.  
Front-line soldiers spent days in the front trench. Then they moved back to support trenches, then reserve trenches.  
Behind the reserves were artillery positions.  
Further back were field hospitals and villages.

Life in the trenches was hard and boring. Death was always close, just above the trench edge. It rained often. Trenches filled with thick mud. Soldiers laid wooden planks on the ground to help. But feet and legs stayed wet. This caused a condition called trench foot. Skin would rot, split, and peel off. It was very painful and hard to prevent.  
Trenches also collected trash and debris. Disease spread easily in the close, dirty space.

Sometimes, soldiers from both sides spoke across no-man’s land. An example happened in December 1914, the first Christmas of the war. German and British soldiers called out to each other. First one side sang carols, then the other. Slowly, some climbed out of their trenches. They met in the middle ground between them. There, they shared cigarettes, candy, and small souvenirs. Many soldiers wrote about similar moments. This Christmas truce showed human kindness during war. But leaders at headquarters did not allow it to happen again.

Other battles were not always in trenches.  
Italian and Austro-Hungarian troops fought in the high Alps mountains. Soldiers faced thin air, little food, and deep snow. Frostbite and avalanches were real dangers. More than half the casualties here came from cold and snow, not just bullets. Narrow mountain passes also made retreat hard.

Fighting began in 1914 between Russians and Ottomans in the Caucasus. The area was isolated. Ottoman forces lacked good roads to bring supplies far from the front. Deep snow and temperatures below freezing made travel hard. Without enough food and supplies, Ottoman troops suffered many casualties—tens of thousands.

In dry places like the Mediterranean and Middle East, armies needed water. Finding enough water for people and animals was difficult. Horses needed feed, which was scarce. In the Middle East especially, soldiers used camels more to carry supplies and people. Camels handled the desert heat better than horses.

**Soil Erosion and Water in West Africa (Dyslexia-Friendly Version)**

8.  **Building lines along field slopes—contours and tie ridges—helps save water.** It also slows down fast runoff across the land. Using both contour lines and tie ridges together works well.
9.  **These earthworks are simple, effective ways to manage water and reduce soil erosion.** But farmers must consider local soil types when using them. **The Jakhanke Islamic Movement in West Africa**

A history of Islam in West Africa must include the Jakhanke movement. It began in the 12th century. Its leader was Alhajj Salim Suwareh. He helped spread Islam in present-day Mali, Guinea, Senegal, and The Gambia. These four countries are still among the most Islamic in West Africa today.

The Jakhanke work did produce strong results. But first: who were they? Why do we study them when looking at how Islam spread in West Africa?

A respected Gambian historian, Lamin Sanneh (the main expert on the Jakhanke), describes them as a "specialized group" of Muslim teachers and scholars. The word "caste" might suggest they belonged to a larger ethnic group called Serahuli. Serahuli is also written as Soninke in some books. Today, people often call them Mandinka. They speak a type of Mandinka language. But this happened mainly because Mandinka chiefs welcomed the Jakhanke when they moved from present-day Mali to the Senegambia region (Senegal and The Gambia). So their connection to Mandinka culture came later, through living with Mandinka chiefs. As teachers and scholars, the Jakhanke were literate. This let them teach Islam and do missionary work.

This is why the Jakhanke matter. They spread Islam peacefully in Senegambia. This is especially important now. Today, many parts of the world see violent acts linked to Islam. The peaceful methods the Jakhanke used long ago are worth remembering. Much of how Islam was later taught calmly and effectively in Senegambia comes from their example. In short: they set early standards for peaceful missionary work.

What were these standards?  
*   They always chose a peaceful way to share Islam. They did not use fighting or swords to spread the religion.  
*   Instead, they used calm methods:  
    *   Building Koranic schools and mosques.  
    *   Improving existing mosques.  
    *   Holding regular sessions to explain the Koran.  
    *   Protecting holy places where people gather yearly for Islamic events.  
    *   Being traders who taught Islam while doing business with clients and customers.  

The Jakhanke also had clear tactics:  
*   They valued having many followers (talibes or disciples). Disciples studied with them for years. After learning, they could go out and gather new disciples themselves. This helped grow their numbers and strengthen Islam.  
*   They often moved to quiet places far from busy towns. They liked peaceful, isolated areas—like religious villages deep in the Senegambian savanna. There, they built self-sustaining communities focused on Islamic study and practice. Villages like Sutukuho (Sutukung) in The Gambia, and Niokhlo and Suna Karantba in Casamance (Southern Senegal) still exist as examples of this.

We have not yet spoken about Alhaji Salim Suwareh. He founded the Jakhanke movement we discussed above. His role was key to its success. We should look at him briefly.

Details about his early life are unclear. But some important points survive:  
*   He died around 1500.  
*   He is said to have made seven trips to Mecca (the hajj). He had relatives there and may have lived there before moving to West Africa to spread Islam.  
*   After his seventh trip, he stayed in Africa. He settled in the Jaka region of Masina, which is now in Mali. This is likely where "Jakhanke" comes from: it means "people from Jaka" in Mandinka language.  
*   When an animist ruler in Bambuku (also in present-day Mali) became hostile to them, Suwareh followed the example of the Prophet Muhammad when Meccans threw stones at him: he left with his group of disciples and went into exile.  
*   He led his followers from Jaka Masina towards present-day Senegambia. Historian Professor Sanneh writes that since this journey (like a hijra, or sacred flight), the Jakhanke have been united by strong loyalty to Suwareh’s teachings and way of life.

The Jakhanke were deeply committed to peaceful spreading of Islam. For example: when a Serahuli religious leader named Momodou Lamin Drammeh (1835–1887) decided to wage war to convert Bundu (in eastern Senegal), the main Jakhanke groups rejected him. They moved further south, into present-day eastern Gambia. Drammeh’s violent style was very different from the Jakhanke’s calm, orderly methods of spreading Islam. Without using swords, the Jakhanke successfully spread and strengthened Islam—unlike jihadist leaders such as Umar Taal or Maba Jahou Bah.  

This can seem surprising. Suwareh lived in Mecca and had relatives there. He would have known strict Wahhabi teachings. Why then did the Jakhanke follow a "path of accommodation" instead of that uncompromising view? The answer may not be obvious, but it is clear: they chose peace over force from the start.

**In summary: What does the Jakhanke movement mean?**  
The Jakhanke showed how Islam could spread peacefully, led by communities and teachers. Their way had a deep, lasting impact on the societies who accepted Islam—showing it as a way of peace. People today who claim to spread Islam through violence may learn from this older example. The Jakhanke movement began over 500 years ago and offers a clear historical model of peaceful Islamic propagation.

**European Contact with Sub-Saharan Africa (to 1650)**

Portuguese sailors first reached sub-Saharan Africa in 1442. They sailed to the Senegal River.  
Before this, since 1413, Portuguese ships had been sailing along Morocco and Western Sahara coasts. In 1413, they captured the city of Ceuta (which is still Spanish today).  

Between 1413 and the 1440s, the Portuguese built several fortified settlements on the Moroccan coast. Key places were Arzila, Mogador (now called Essaouira), Safi, and Tangier.  
Portugal kept a strong presence in Morocco until 1578. That year, King Sebastião I of Portugal and much of his nobility died at the Battle of Alcácer-Quibir.  

By 1471, West African leaders from Senegal to Ghana had made trade and diplomatic contacts with Portuguese traders. Early main trade and settlement sites included places along the Gambia River, Bugendo on the São Domingos River in Guinea-Bissau, and Sierra Leone.  

For the next 150 years, West African rulers and traders met Portuguese more often than any other Europeans.  
English and French traders also had smaller missions, but these were less common.  

In the beginning, Portugal’s main reasons for coming were:  
1. They wanted gold from Bono-Mansu and Akan states.  
2. They competed with the Ottoman Empire for this gold (the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453, causing a crisis in Christian Europe).  
3. They sought a sea route to India around the Cape of Good Hope.  
4. Over time, they increasingly traded enslaved people.  

By the 1590s, Dutch ships began to rival Portuguese ships as the main European traders in Africa.  
Dutch ships were larger and better built. The goods they offered African leaders were often higher quality than what the Portuguese offered.  
By 1650, the Dutch had captured many key Portuguese trading stations. This included Gorée in Senegal (1621), Elmina in Ghana (1637), and Luanda in Angola (1641).  

At first, the Dutch mainly traded for textiles, animal hides (for leather), and ivory.  
But by the mid-17th century, they also began trading enslaved people themselves.  
Dutch interest in slave trading started in the 1620s. This was linked to them capturing part of Portuguese Brazil that year.  
From 1630 to 1654, the Dutch controlled northern Brazil and its sugar plantations, which used enslaved labor.  
Their growing colonial interests increased their involvement in slave trading. This became dominant in trade during the second half of the 18th century.  

In the second half of the 17th century, other European nations began this pattern too.  
Danish, English, French, German, and Swedish traders set up trading posts (called "factories") at various places in West Africa.  
This deepened African-European trade and interaction.  

This chapter focuses on the early period of African-European contact, up to 1650.  
It looks at this time before the trade in enslaved persons became the main part of trade.  
A later chapter will cover the trans-Atlantic slave trade in more detail.

**Portuguese Exploration in West Africa (1442–1510s)**

*   Portuguese ships reached the Senegal River in 1442.
*   Their voyages continued after this.
*   By 1448, some sailors sailed up the Gambia River.
*   They reached Kantora, a major trading town near today’s Basse Santa Su (in eastern Senegal).
*   Kantora was important for trans-Saharan trade at that time.
*   In the mid-1450s, trade began with the Wolof state of Kajoor on the coast.
*   The Bijagós Islands (off Guinea-Bissau) also started talks with European traders.
*   People likely first spoke Arabic to each other.
*   Many Portuguese knew Arabic in the 1500s. Granada was still an Islamic kingdom in Spain then.
*   Arabic was widely spoken across West Africa too.
*   A sailor wrote in 1456: the Bijagós were the last place where Africans shared a language with Portuguese sailors.
*   This suggests Arab and trans-Saharan trade probably did not go further south at that time.
*   The Cape Verde Islands were likely first reached around 1456.
*   Some historians debate if people lived there already. Archaeology does not give clear proof.
*   The islands might have been a salt depot for Saharan states.
*   Around 1471, Portuguese ships reached the coast of Ghana.
*   Ghana’s coastline was close to Akan gold mines in the forests.
*   Akan traders soon sold gold informally to Portuguese sailors.
*   The Portuguese government wanted its share of this trade.
*   In 1481, they sent a large fleet to Edina (now called Elmina).
*   They negotiated with Kwamena Ansa, the ruler there, to build a fortress.
*   Talks were tense. This started when the Portuguese tried to build their fort at a sacred site.
*   After talks ended, the fortress at Elmina was built.
*   It still stands today on what became known as the Gold Coast.
*   Later, in the 1600s, the Dutch took over this fortress.
*   In time, the Dutch and English became the main European traders in Ghana.
*   Much trade happened on the Gold Coast.
*   Many Akan rulers wanted to expand their own trading links.
*   The Portuguese built more forts along the Gold Coast, such as Axim and Komenda.
*   Most of these were finished by 1500.
*   More forts were built later, often every few miles along the coast.
*   Some forts traded only gold. Others, like Anishan, traded corn, which Europeans also wanted.
*   The slave trade did not become the main trade on the Gold Coast until the 1700s.
*   Meanwhile, other West and West-Central African rulers met Portuguese sailors.
*   Oba Ozolua of Benin welcomed Portuguese visitors in 1485.
*   An Atlantic trading post called Gwatón was set up around 1490.
*   Benin first sold malaguetta pepper to the Portuguese.
*   In 1499, a sea route to India opened.
*   Demand for Benin’s pepper in Europe then fell.
*   The Portuguese tried to send enslaved people from Benin to Elmina (for gold).
*   The Oba refused this request.
*   Over the 1500s, Benin’s contact with Portugal slowly decreased.
*   In the early 1600s, Benin Obas made new links with European traders. This was because the Dutch wanted Benin cloth.
*   Cloth remained Benin’s main export throughout the 1500s.
*   Ambassy cloths were traded regularly to Elmina and as far as Brazil.
*   Demand for Benin cloth fell in the late 1500s.
*   This happened because luxury cloths from India became more popular.
*   By the 1700s, Benin Obas had to turn to the trade in enslaved persons. They did this to keep and rebuild the power of Edo and the Benin state.
*   Portuguese ships kept sailing south after Benin.
*   They reached the mouth of the Kongo River.
*   They made contact with Nzika Nkuwu, the manikongo (king) at Mbanza Kongo (the capital).
*   The island of São Tomé was settled by 1485.
*   Many BaKongo people were taken there as enslaved persons to work on sugar plantations.
*   In 1491, Nzika Nkuwu converted to Christianity. He took the name João I.
*   This led to trade links between Kongo, São Tomé, and Elmina.
*   By the 1510s, traders from Benin were present at the Kongolese port of Mpinda.

*   Therefore, by the 1510s, many different West African peoples and their rulers had contact with the Portuguese.
*   Some, like Benin and Elmina, also linked further south to Kongo.
*   African rulers wanted more trading contacts.
*   At times, they also sought military support against rivals.
*   For example, Benin used Portuguese help in a major battle against Nupe in 1516.
*   Civil wars in Jolof and Kongo also saw such requests for support.

**Missionaries and Health Services**

Before Christian missionaries arrived, most sick people relied on traditional medicine. They used herbs, roots, and tree bark for cures. Modern science now confirms many of these have real medicinal value. However, traditional practice had serious problems.  

Preventive medicine was rarely known. This meant epidemics happened often. Traditional doctors also struggled to diagnose illness correctly. They sometimes thought natural sickness came from spirits. They might use mystic rituals before giving medicine. They also gave many rules (taboos) that modern medicine knows do not help the patient.  

Christian missionaries changed this. They started medical centres, first at their mission posts. Later, they built more centres across different areas to care for the sick. In time, they also built leprosariums and orphanages to support their medical work.  

**Examples in Nigeria:**  
*   Roman Catholics were among the first to start organised medical services.  
*   Father Jean Marie Coquard worked in Abeokuta for 40 years (second half of the 1800s). The Egba people knew him as both a priest and a surgeon.  
*   In 1892, the Church Missionary Society opened Iyi Enu Hospital in Onitsha. It is now a leading hospital in Anambra State.  
*   In 1902, Methodists opened a clinic at Igbo-Ora.  
*   Mary Slessor, a Scottish missionary, was known as a nurse in the Cross River area. She worked hard to stop people from killing twins.  
*   J. R. Stephen led a missionary hospital at Ilesha for many years.  
*   Many more mission hospitals were built across West Africa during the 1900s.  

**Examples in Ghana:**  
*   Missionaries in Ghana also started medical services early, like in Nigeria.  
*   Roman Catholic Sisters provided medical care in the Upper and Northern Regions before the government built its own hospitals.  
*   In the Western Region, Sisters at Eikwe’s hospital focused on maternity (pregnancy and birth). Like Mary Slessor in Nigeria, they stopped the practice of killing twins at birth.  
*   Roman Catholic hospitals were built in all nine regions:  
    *   Asikuma and Foso (Central Region)  
    *   Akyem Swedru (Eastern Region)  
    *   Berekum (Brong-Ahafo Region)  
    *   Maase (Asante Region)  
    *   Anfoega (Volta Region)  
*   Presbyterians also opened hospitals, including one at Agogo in Asante-Akyem.  
*   Other well-known long-standing missionary hospitals include:  
    *   Methodists at Wenkyi (Brong-Ahafo Region)  
    *   Seventh Day Adventists at Kwahu Atibie (Eastern Region)

### Impact of World War II on West Africa

World War Two speeded up nationalism. It weakened imperialism. The war had big economic effects on West Africa.

**1. West Africa became more important to world trade.**  
Europe needed more rubber, cotton, cocoa, palm oil, and groundnuts from tropical Africa. Colonial governments pushed colonies to grow more cash crops.  
In Nigeria:  
* Exports rose from 10,300,00 pounds in 1931 to 24,600,00 pounds in 1946.  
* Imports rose from 6,800,00 pounds to 19,800,00 pounds in the same period.  

**2. Workers had growing complaints.**  
The colonial government:  
* Controlled prices.  
* Controlled how export crops were sold.  
* Set maximum wages.  
* Pressed for higher production.  
African businessmen could not join import or export trade. Only European firms could do this work.

**3. Trade unions grew quickly.**  
Cost of living rose, but wages did not rise as fast. This pushed workers to organize.  
In Nigeria:  
* The number of trade unions went from 5 to 70.  
* The Nigerian Trade Union Congress (formed in 1943) became the main group linking all unions.  
Unions worked closely with nationalist leaders for an end to colonial rule.

**4. Cities grew fast because of jobs.**  
Many people moved to cities for work. Several West African cities more than doubled in size.  
* Lagos: 100,000 in 1939 → 230,00 in 1950.  
* Accra: 70,000 in 1941 → 166,00 in 1948.  
Cities became crowded. Job seekers and workers saw Europeans living in comfortable areas with paved streets and gardens. They lived in slums themselves. This made people more open to nationalist ideas. They became the first willing members of militant nationalist groups.

**5. War helped education grow.**  
War time brought more money to West Africa. More parents could afford school fees. Literacy increased. More people read newspapers.  
Nationalists used newspapers to call for political, economic, and social change.

**6. Many young people stayed unemployed.**  
Even with new jobs, thousands of school leavers had no work. Cities now had a large group of unemployed people. They blamed the colonial government and European firms. Nationalist agitators could easily get their support.

**7. The biggest reason for faster nationalism: returning ex-servicemen.**  
Over 176,000 men from British West Africa served in the colonial army during the war. After the war, many returned home.  
* About 100,000 returned to Nigeria.  
* About 65,000 returned to Ghana (from the Middle East, East Africa, Burma, and India).  
These ex-servicemen had seen life in other countries. They lived well in the army. They saw strong nationalist movements in Asia. They fought alongside Europeans and saw their weaknesses. This broke the idea that Europeans were naturally superior.

### Collecting Data for African History

To write accurate African history, historians must use many kinds of evidence. They cannot rely only on written records or unwritten traditions. Using several methods helps find and correct bias, prejudice, and exaggeration.

#### Method 1: Personal Enquiry and Interview  
Historians talk directly to people who know about the past. These may include elders, traditional historians, court officials, or eye-witnesses. The historian asks clear questions about a community’s culture and history. Interviews can be recorded, written down later, and carefully studied. This gives first-hand information from living memory.

#### Method 2: Inter-disciplinary Work  
Historians work with experts in other fields. Linguists, archaeologists, botanists, ethnographers, and others help gather evidence. For example:  
*   Linguists study language clues about history.  
*   Archaeologists find physical remains like tools or buildings.  
*   Botanists identify plants used historically.  
Together, this wider team builds stronger, fuller histories.

#### Method 3: Reviewing Written Sources  
Historians examine books, newspapers, journals, diaries, letters, broadcasts, and manifestos. They check both primary sources (from the time) and secondary sources (written later). Written records have limits—they may be incomplete or biased. But historians compare them carefully. This helps ensure their history is fair and based on proof.

#### Method 4: Using Questionnaires  
To gather good information, historians create clear question sets. Questions cover key areas: politics, economy, society, religion, and technology. These questions are given to people who know the past. Answers are collected and analyzed to reach sound conclusions. This makes sure important topics are not missed.

#### Method 5: Personal Observation and Records  
Historians visit places with historical meaning: slave trade sites, forts, castles, or villages. They watch events like festivals or funerals happen. They write down what they see immediately. These notes are first-hand accounts—they saw the event themselves. Other sources can then be compared to these observations for a clearer picture.

#### Reliability of Written and Unwritten Sources  

**Written sources** (books, letters, diaries, etc.) often give precise details. Historians use scientific methods when reviewing them: comparing, cross-checking, and testing evidence. This reduces bias and helps find truth. When combined with other evidence, written records support strong conclusions.

**Unwritten sources** (oral tradition, archaeology) are also reliable when used properly. They need careful research too.  
*   **Oral tradition:** Elders share history through stories. Linguists like Professor Abena Dolphyne studied Asante, Bono, and Fante languages. She found the Asante language is less closely related to Fante than thought. However, oral accounts can sometimes exaggerate or focus on certain topics (like wars or famous people) while missing social or economic details. Memory loss can also affect specific facts. Historians must ask careful questions and compare stories from many people.  
*   **Archaeology:** This is a main source for African history. Archaeologists use scientific methods: walking areas to find sites, digging carefully (stratification), and using tests like radiocarbon dating or potassium-argon dating. These methods give accurate results about age and place. But archaeology has limits:  
*   There is often no system to save old objects or places on purpose—finds can be accidental.  
*   Objects wear down from weather, time, or damage, making them hard to study fully.  
*   Dating tests are expensive and not always possible for every find.  

#### Conclusion: Using All Evidence Together  

Both written records and unwritten traditions (like oral history and archaeology) must be used together in African history. Neither is perfect on its own because all sources come from people, who can have personal views or limits. Written sources need checking against other evidence. Unwritten sources also need careful testing and comparison. By combining methods—interviews, interdisciplinary work, reviewing written records, questionnaires, observation, archaeology—historians build the most reliable and balanced history possible. This respects all kinds of knowledge and avoids relying too much on one single source.

5.  **Minimal Jargon/Abbreviations:** Fully spelled out terms (e.g., "radiocarbon dating" not just "radiocarbon"; "stratification" explained in context). Avoided acronyms entirely.

text:
Here is a revised version of the chapter, rewritten to be more readable and dyslexia-accessible. It uses clear, short sentences, avoids complex vocabulary where possible, maintains precise facts and timelines, and structures information logically for easier reading:

**West Africa and the Mediterranean World: Early Connections**

People in West Africa have been connected to the Mediterranean world for a very long time. These links are older than the start of Islam in the late 600s CE.

Long before the Roman Empire began, the Greek writer Herodotus (around 484–425 BCE) wrote about people in Africa. He often described people along the Nile River as Black Africans. He also suggested they were connected to groups further west.

Rock paintings from this time and later show wheeled chariots south of today’s Sahara Desert. This suggests trade or contact with the Mediterranean world.

The Sahara was not always a harsh desert. Many centuries ago, it was wetter and more fertile. Rock paintings in the Sahara are common. Some are over 12,000 years old. Good examples are:
*   Tassili n’Ajjer, north of Tamanrasset in Algeria.
*   The Tibesti Massif in Chad.
These old paintings show areas now desert as green and rich with animals. These animals include buffalo, elephant, rhino, and hippo. They cannot live there today. This wetter time happened while Europe was in an Ice Age. But Africa had plenty of water and food then.

Around 3000 years ago (c. 3000 BCE), the Sahara began drying out faster. However, strong links with the Mediterranean continued for many more years.

One clear example is Hannibal. He was a Carthaginian general from Libya. Around 220 BCE, he led an attack on Roman forces in Europe. His army crossed the high Alps mountains. They used African elephants for supplies and transport. These elephants came from south of the Sahara.

As the desert grew larger, crossing it became harder. By the time Islam began (around 610 CE), fewer direct links remained. But new connections grew later. The rise of strong Islamic kingdoms in Morocco, and learning centers in Cairo, Tripoli, and the Middle East, led to a growing caravan trade across the Sahara.

By the 900s CE, the Kingdom of Ghana (also called Awkar) was established in what is now Mauritania. Early writings about it start around 830 CE. Its capital city was Koumbi-Saleh. Trade routes from Ghana focused on western Sahara, ending at Sijilmasa.

By the 1000s CE, Koumbi-Saleh had separate areas for people practicing African religions and Muslims. This shows many North African traders were visiting. Gold trade was already important in Mediterranean commerce. Around 1000 CE, West African gold was first made into coins for European markets.

By the 1100s CE, events in West Africa were closely linked to North Africa and Europe. A major change happened then. The Almoravid movement began. They were Berber Muslims. They likely moved north from near the Senegal River. This happened after the middle of the 11th century. They sought a stricter form of Islam.
They conquered Morocco. They founded Marrakech in 1062. In the 1080s, they entered southern Spain (Al-Andalus). They defended the Caliphate of Córdoba from Christian Spanish kings trying to take it back. Córdoba had split into small states called Taifa kingdoms by the 1030s. Later, in the 1200s, the Almohads (also from Morocco) defeated the Almoravids and took over in 1147.

In West Africa, big changes happened in Ghana first. Until 1076, Muslims and people of African religions lived together there. But in 1076, Almoravid raiders attacked and sacked the city. Ghana declined after this. The Mali Empire did not rise until the 1300s.

Gold trade became the main part of Sahara crossing trade. Money was a key reason Arabic traders first came to West Africa. They called it "the golden country."
The effect of this gold trade on Europe is clear. For example, the Spanish word for a gold coin in the 15th century, *maravedí*, comes from an Almoravid coin called the *murabitūn dinar*.

Gold trade helped powerful empires grow: Mali, Bono-Mansu, and Songhay. It also grew cities like Kano. Trading groups like the Wangara became important. Arabic became more widely used as Islam spread. It was used for writing laws and records.

By the 1400s CE, when Atlantic Ocean trade began, the Sahara crossing trade had been strong for at least 500 years. This trade had already helped shape many West African states and societies—their rise, decline, and growth.

introduction west africa and the mediterranean world links

people in west africa have been connected to the mediterranean world for a very long time. these links are older than the start of islam in the late 600s ce. people travelled and traded across large distances. this happened before roman times began.  

ancient evidence from rock paintings

rock paintings show wheeled chariots south of today s sahara desert. these suggest trade or contact with the mediterranean world. some rock paintings are over twelve thousand years old. good examples are tassili n ajjer in algeria and the tibesti massif in chad.  

these old paintings show areas now desert as green and rich. they show animals like buffalo elephant rhino and hippo. these animals cannot live there today. this wetter time happened while europe was in an ice age. africa had plenty of water and food then.  

the saharan climate long ago

around three thousand years ago which is about 3000 bce the sahara began drying out faster. but strong links with the mediterranean continued for many more years. crossing the desert became harder as it grew larger. by the time islam began around 610 ce fewer direct links remained.  

hannibal and early trade connections

one clear example is hanibal. he was a carthaginian general from libya. around 220 bce he led an attack on roman forces in europe. his army crossed the high alps mountains. they used african elephants for supplies and transport. these elephants came from south of the sahara desert.  

trade grows in west africa after 830 ce

by the 900s ce the kingdom of ghana was established in what is now mauritania. early writings about it start around 830 ce. its capital city was koumbi saleh. trade routes from ghana focused on western sahara ending at sijilmasa.  

by the 1000s ce koumbi saleh had separate areas for people practicing african religions and muslims. this shows many north african traders were visiting. gold trade was already important in mediterranean commerce. around 1000 ce west african gold was first made into coins for european markets.  

the almoravid movement and its effects

a major change happened in the 1100s ce. the almoravid movement began. they were berber muslims. they likely moved north from near the senegal river after the middle of the 11th century. they sought a stricter form of islam.  

they conquered morocco. they founded marakech in 1062. in the 1080s they entered southern spain al andalus. they defended the caliphate of cordoba from christian spanish kings trying to take it back. cordoba had split into small states called taifa kingdoms by the 1030s. later in the 1200s the almohads also from morocco defeated the almoravids and took over in 1147.  

in west africa big changes happened in ghana first. until 1076 muslims and people of african religions lived together there. but in 1076 almoravid raiders attacked and sacked the city. ghana declined after this. the mali empire did not rise until the 1300s.  

gold trade shapes empires and cities

gold trade became the main part of saharan crossing trade. money was a key reason arabic traders first came to west africa. they called it the golden country.  

the effect of this gold trade on europe is clear. for example the spanish word for a gold coin in the 15th century maravedi comes from an almoravid coin called the murabitun dinar.  

gold trade helped powerful empires grow mali bono mansu and songhay. it also grew cities like kano. trading groups like the wangara became important. arabic became more widely used as islam spread. it was used for writing laws and records.  

summary of trans saharan trade by the 1400s

by the 1400s ce when atlantic ocean trade began the saharan crossing trade had been strong for at least five hundred years. this trade had already helped shape many west african states and societies. it shaped their rise decline and growth.

**Mali and Mansa Musa: The Trans-Saharan Trade**

The most famous kingdom linked to trans-Saharan trade was Mali.  
Mali was founded in the 13th century by Sunjata Keita. He defeated King Sumanguru Kante, who was a blacksmith ruler.  

Within Mali, Emperor Mansa Musa became world-renowned.  
His full name was Mansa Kankan Musa Keita.  
He ruled from 1312 to 1337. His reign lasted about 25 years.  
But the whole 1300s are still called "the Century of Mansa Musa" because of his lasting legacy.  

Mansa Musa’s son was born to Mansa Aboubacarr II, known as "the Navigator."  
In the 1300s, Aboubacarr sent an expedition across the Atlantic Ocean.  
It started from the River Gambia area. The goal was to find new lands.  

Mansa Musa’s most famous act was his pilgrimage to Mecca.  
This journey happened in 1324 and 1325.  
He did not plan to go at first. He was only a nominal Muslim then.  
But after accidentally killing his mother, he decided to make the Hajj.  
He wanted to purify himself and make amends for this serious act.  

Mansa Musa took his whole court with him on this trip.  
This included doctors, princes, griots (storytellers), and an army of 8,000 bodyguards.  
They left the Malian capital. They traveled across the Sahara.  
Their route went through Walata (in present-day Mauretania), then Libya, then Cairo.  
From Cairo, they entered Mecca, the holy city.  

This pilgrimage had three big effects: economic, religious, and political.  

**Economic Effects:**  
Mansa Musa gave out so much gold during his journey that people still call him the richest person who ever lived.  
He also made strong trade ties between Mali and places like the Middle East and Cairo.  
Because of this, starting in 1325, caravans with over 10,000 camels regularly crossed the Sahara into Mali at Gao and Timbuktu.  

**Religious Effects:**  
Mansa Musa and his large group returned from Mecca as stronger Muslims.  
They wanted to spread Islam widely.  
Most Malians at that time were animists (believing in spirits of nature).  
The returning pilgrims helped convert many people to Islam.  
Arab scholars also came to Mali because of Mansa Musa’s great wealth.  
These Arabs built fine mosques and royal courts for him.  
Mansa Musa also brought back great scholars. They helped start the famous libraries in Gao, Jenne, and Timbuktu.  
His journey made Mali very well known all over the world.  

**Political Effects:**  
Mali became clearly on the map because of Mansa Musa’s fame.  
Before he died in 1337, Mansa Musa had grown Mali into a large empire.  
This empire included over 400 cities.  
It stretched from the Atlantic Ocean in the west to forest areas in the south.  
All major states of that time were part of Mansa Musa’s Mali. These included Songhay, Ghana, Galam, and Tekrur.  

Mansa Musa gave Mali its great glory during his rule.  
At the same time, Mali gave Mansa Musa his great fame.

### West African Changes in the 15th Century: Trade and Power

Trans-Saharan trade grew strongly from the 10th to the 15th century. This trade caused many changes across West Africa. These changes happened clearly in the 15th century. They affected areas from west to east, and from north to south.

West African changes—political, economic, and social—drove global links. These changes also shaped Europe’s role later on. It was not the other way around: Europe did not cause these West African changes first.

**Changes in Nigeria:**
In Borno, gold trade from Bono-Mansu grew. This led to a move. The capital moved south. It left the old centre of Kanem. The new capital was Gazargamo (Ngazargamu) in Borno. This happened around 1470.

In Kano, a new system started. It was called the Sarauta system.

Earthworks called "Eredos" are near Ijebu in Yorubaland. They are about 10 metres deep. Archaeologist Gérard Chouin dated them recently. He found they were built between 1370 and 1420.

**Changes in other regions:**
In Mali, the Dogon people likely moved to the Bandiagara escarpment in the 15th century.

In what is now Burkina Faso, the Mossi kingdom rose in the 15th century. They earned money by taxing gold moving through their land. Al-Sa’dī wrote about Mossi attacking Mâssina during this time.

Bono-Mansu also grew in power during this century.

On the Gold Coast, a key gold-trading centre called Bighu (called Bito by al-Ouazzan) is mentioned in the 1520s. This shows it became important in these decades. It would become very major later, in the 17th and 18th centuries.

**Changes in Senegambia:**
At the end of the 15th century, Koli Tenguela rose as a major military leader. This probably happened while trying to control gold trade from Wuuli (on the north bank of the Gambia River). Tenguela was Fula. He led an army south across the Gambia River. They went to the Fuuta Jaalo mountains in Guinea-Conakry. There, he started a new polity. This later led to the establishment of Fuuta Tooro on the Senegal River.

**Summary: West Africa First:**
All across West Africa—from Borno to Fuuta Tooro—political changes were happening. These happened well before regular trade with Europe began. West African mining, economic shifts, and government reorganization grew strong. This created the situation Europeans later saw when they started sailing along the West African coast in the 15th century.

**Example: Kano’s Growth:**
Kano grew very fast in the 15th century. It sent military expeditions south. Kano became a regional hub. It linked trading networks from southern Nigeria to Mali and beyond. The Kano Chronicle describes these changes. It tells of links between Kano and Nupe province during Sarkin Dauda’s reign (c. 1421-38). Zaria was the major power between Kano and Nupe. Under Queen Amina, Zaria conquered lands up to Kwararafa and Nupe. Every town paid her tribute. The Sarkin Nupe sent forty eunuchs and ten thousand kolas. Over time, products from the west came to Hausaland (of which Kano was the capital).

**Conclusion:**
As European power began expanding along the West African coast in the 15th century, trans-Saharan trade reached its highest point. The 15th century was not only about European expansion. It was a time of global growth: stronger trade networks, production, and power. This power showed clearly in more complex states across West Africa and beyond.

conclusion  

as european power began expanding along the west african coast in the 15th century trans-saharan trade reached its highest point. the 15th century was not only about european expansion. it was a time of global growth stronger trade networks production and power. this power showed clearly in more complex states across west africa and beyond.

### Usman dan Fodio and the Jihad: Key Reasons and Historical Views

**Main Reason for the Jihad**  
Usman dan Fodio started the jihad to purify Islam in territories that were already Muslim by the early 1800s. He believed Muslim leaders before this time had practiced an impure form of Islam. This belief gave his struggle its main justification.

**Religious Focus**  
Dan Fodio stated clearly that religion was the main origin of the jihad. He wrote this in his book *Kitab al-Farq*. Letters he sent to the leader of Borno in the 1800s also show this view. Dan Fodio aimed to reform lax Muslims using pure Muslims. Religion was the central reason, though not the only one.

**Social and Political Context**  
Some historians note that Hausa kingdoms had large social and economic inequalities at the start of the 1800s. Dan Fodio spoke often about equality and fighting corruption. As someone who claimed to represent the people, he began his fight against the king and aristocracy of Gobir in 1804. The social issues were real, but dan Fodio himself emphasized religion as the origin.

**Ethnic Background Clarification**  
Many leaders of the Sokoto jihad were Fulani. Some later historians (in the 1970s) suggested this showed an ethnic conflict: Fulani against Hausa. However, Fulani people were a minority in the region. It is unlikely they launched a major war based only on ethnicity. Dan Fodio himself wrote against any ethnic discrimination in his treatise *Bayan Wayan Wujub al-Hijra*.

**Not a Completely New Idea**  
Discussions about Islam’s role in society happened before dan Fodio’s jihad. People debated rules about food, marriage, and women’s clothing. One scholar, Shaikh Jibril b. 'Umar (dan Fodio’s teacher), focused on women’s dress. Other jihads for religious reform had already taken place in West Africa: Bundu (late 1600s), Futa Jallon (1725), and Futa Toro (1776). So, religious questioning was not new; many Muslim scholars had been reformers before dan Fodio.

**Lasting Impact**  
The religious ideas behind dan Fodio’s jihad were not entirely original. However, his success came from winning political control over a large area. This long-term political victory ensured the lasting influence of his movement.

### The Early Sokoto Caliphate (1804–1810)

The first six years of the jihad were important. They built a new political and religious base. This was not an empire. It was many territories under one caliph in Sokoto.

The Sokoto Caliphate was a new kind of state for Hausa areas. It gave moral and political power to Usman dan Fodio and his successors. Fulani scholars who joined the jihad became emirs. Each emir ruled one territory. They reported directly to the caliph in Sokoto.

The caliphate was large. It split into two parts:  
* Western emirates under Sokoto’s direct rule.  
* Eastern emirates that were more independent.  

Successors of dan Fodio had to fight often. They needed to show their authority. Because of this, jihad almost never stopped until the mid-1800s.

Usman dan Fodio’s son was Mohammed Bello. He became sultan after his father. Bello led many military campaigns. He compared them to early Muslim conquests in Arabia.  

Bello’s policy had three parts:  
1.  He put family members in charge of border towns.  
2.  He settled Fulani nomads in villages.  
3.  He built guarded villages near borders.  

This made border security important. It also mattered between emirates. Soldiers recruited in the dry season helped Sokoto stop rebellions. They also stopped attacks from Tuareg people in the north.

The caliph’s power came from three things:  
* Controlling the borders.  
* Sharing war spoils or taxes with allies and family.  
* Replacing old Hausa leader taxes with Islamic taxes like zakat.  

Islamic law said how these taxes should be used. But each emirate set its own tax rules. For example, Kano and Zaria had a property tax not found in Sokoto’s area.  

Sokoto could not fully control all other areas. Old Hausa town structures limited it. It also could not reach many rural people easily. So central power was limited outside Sokoto’s close emirates.

The caliphate wanted Islamic law in all courts. This needed educated men. Schools started to grow in towns. Early years had few teachers, though.  

A key feature of the Caliphate was its literate staff. These men worked in each emirate’s administration. They were free or had been enslaved. Together, they formed a working government system.

There was not enough local labour. This led to many slave-capturing expeditions. Slaves were sold or forced to work.  
* Salt mines in the north used slave labour heavily.  
* Iron, cotton, indigo, and leather workshops in central areas also relied on slaves.  

Much of the state’s wealth came from this system. It depended on war raids for slaves.  

North African traders brought slaves to Kano in the 1820s. Records show: for every free person, there were thirty enslaved people in the city.

Islam had entered Hausa lands by the 1400s. Travelers and traders from Borno or across the Sahara brought it. Pre-Islamic traditional religions stayed too. But Islamic culture spread widely. Books written by dan Fodio’s family or sold in Sahara trade helped. Pilgrimages to Mecca, trade, and Muslim brotherhoods also connected Hausa areas to the wider Muslim world. The jihad made this connection faster and stronger. Integration existed before, but the jihad greatly increased it.

    *   "virtually uninterrupted phenomenon" → "almost never stopped until the mid-1800s"

    *   "pre-jihadic structures" → "old Hausa town structures"
    *   "servile economy fuelled by wars or raids" → "Much of the state’s wealth came from this system. It depended on war raids for slaves."
    *   Avoided abstract nouns where possible ("phenomenon", "tendency") in favor of active verbs and clear subjects ("Sokoto could not fully control...").
3.  **Consistent Structure & Predictability:** Used bullet points for lists (Bello’s policy, caliph’s power sources, slave labour examples). This breaks up text visually and makes information easy to scan. All facts about a topic are grouped together logically.
4.  **Avoided Tricky Word Patterns:** Minimized words that look similar but mean different things (e.g., "caliph"/"Caliphate" standardized to "caliph" and "Caliphate"; avoided phrases like "it is worth noting that"). Ensured homographs (words spelled the same but different meaning/context) are unlikely to cause confusion in this context.

**Revised Chapter:**

Al Hajj Umar Tal lived from 1797 to 1864. He was a leader in West Africa. We will look at his life and his jihads (holy wars). First, we focus on his military campaigns in present-day Mali and Guinea Conakry. These took place between 1848 and 1864.

His early campaigns targeted the gold states of Bambuk and Bure. At that time, these areas were ruled by animist Malinke people. Animist means they believed in spirits or nature gods, not Islam.

Between 1848 and 1854, Umar Tal took control of several Malinke communities: Bandjogou, Bougary, and Farabana. All are now in Guinea Conakry. He established the Tijaniya Muslim community there. His first capital was Jalafara. He raised the Tijaniya flag at this site.

After success in Guinea, Umar Tal turned to areas in present-day Mali. He attacked the Bambara rulers of Kaarta and Segou. He also fought the animist Fulani people in Macina. By 1854, he had built a large Muslim state. This state included Kaarta, Segou, Macina, and Khasso. He brought the powerful Bambara army under his Tijaniya leadership.

The respected Malian historian Sekene Mody Cissokho wrote: *“Al Hajj Umar brought Islam to the Western Sudan.”* This highlights his role as both a scholar and a builder of an empire.

Umar Tal’s early achievements were clear. At age 23, in 1820, he finished his religious studies. He earned the title *alfa*, meaning scholar. That same year, he traveled to Mecca for pilgrimage. He stayed in Arabia for 13 years (until 1833). There, he was ordained as a *Kalifa*—an official leader or emissary—of the Tijaniya movement in West Africa. This gave him formal approval to lead jihads later.

During his time in Arabia, he likely visited nearby places like Kanem-Borno and Sokoto. These regions had just completed their own jihads. He may have learned lessons useful for his work in the Sahel region.

Historians note Umar Tal’s main goal was conversion, not destruction. He aimed to bring animist rulers and people into Tijaniya Islam. He also wanted to move those already Muslim (like Qadriya followers) into Tijaniya. His quick success was not only due to military strength. His version of Tijaniya also helped ordinary people. For example, he freed slaves in areas he controlled. He also helped poor and disadvantaged communities meet basic needs like food and shelter.

Umar Tal died in 1864. His death happened at Dinguiray after a battle with French forces. Until then, he was a popular leader—both as a jihadist and as an empire builder.

His son, Amadou Seku, succeeded him as ruler of the Imamate (the Muslim state). However, Amadou Seku struggled to hold together the large territory his father had built.

**European Contact with Sub-Saharan Africa (to 1650)**

Portuguese sailors first reached sub-Saharan Africa in 1442. They sailed to the Senegal River.  
Before this, since 1413, Portuguese ships had been sailing along Morocco and Western Sahara coasts. In 1413, they captured the city of Ceuta. Ceuta is still a Spanish city today.  

Between 1413 and the 1440s, the Portuguese built several fortified settlements on the Moroccan coast. Key places were Arzila, Mogador (now called Essaouira), Safi, and Tangier.  
Portuguese presence in Morocco lasted until 1578. That year, King Sebastião I of Portugal and much of his nobility died at the Battle of Alcácer-Quibir.  

By 1471, West African leaders from Senegal to Ghana had made trade and diplomatic contacts with Portuguese traders. Early main trade places were along the Gambia River, Bugendo on the São Domingos River in Guinea-Bissau, and Sierra Leone.  

For the next 150 years, West African rulers and traders met Portuguese more often than any other Europeans.  
English and French traders also had small missions, but these were less common.  

In the beginning, Portuguese main reasons for coming were:  
1. They wanted gold from Bono-Mansu and Akan states.  
2. They competed with the Ottoman Empire for this gold. The Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453. This caused a crisis in Christian Europe.  
3. They sought a sea route to India around the Cape of Good Hope.  
4. Over time, trade in enslaved people became more important.  

By the 1590s, Dutch ships began to rival Portuguese ships as the main European traders in Africa.  
Dutch ships were larger and better built. The goods they traded with African leaders were higher quality than Portuguese goods.  
By 1650, the Dutch had captured many key Portuguese trading stations. These included:  
* Gorée Island in Senegal (captured in 1621)  
* Elmina in Ghana (captured in 1637)  
* Luanda in Angola (captured in 1641)  

At first, the Dutch mainly traded for textiles, animal hides (for leather), and ivory.  
But by the mid-17th century, they also began trading enslaved people.  
Dutch interest in slave trading started in the 1620s. This followed their capture of part of Portuguese Brazil.  
From 1630 to 1654, the Dutch controlled northern Brazil and its sugar plantations. These plantations used enslaved labour.  
Their growing colonial interests increased their involvement in slave trading. Slave trading became dominant in the second half of the 18th century.  

In the second half of the 17th century, other European nations also began this pattern.  
Danish, English, French, German, and Swedish traders set up trade posts (called "factories") at various places in West Africa.  
This deepened African-European trade and interaction.  

This chapter focuses on the early period of African-European contact, up to 1650.

**Portuguese Exploration in West Africa (1442–1510s)**

Portuguese voyages reached the Senegal River in 1442.  
They continued exploring along the coast.  

By 1448, Portuguese sailors sailed up the Gambia River.  
They reached Kantora, a major trading town.  
Kantora is near today’s Basse Santa Su, in eastern Senegal.  
At that time, Kantora was an important centre for trans-Saharan trade.  

In the mid-1450s, trade began with the Wolof state of Kajoor on the coast.  
The Bijagós Islands (off Guinea-Bissau) also started talks with European traders.  

People likely first spoke Arabic when meeting.  
Many Portuguese knew Arabic in the 1500s.  
Granada was still an Islamic kingdom in Spain then.  
Arabic was also widely used across West Africa.  

In 1456, one sailor wrote about the Bijagós Islands.  
He said this was the last place where Africans shared a language with Portuguese sailors.  
This suggests Arab and trans-Saharan trade likely did not go further south at that time.  

Portuguese probably first reached the Cape Verde Islands around 1456.  
Some historians debate if people lived there already.  
Archaeology has not proven this clearly.  
The islands may have been a salt depot for Saharan states.  

Around 1471, Portuguese explored the coast of Ghana.  
This area was close to Akan gold mines in the forests.  
Akan traders soon sold gold informally to Portuguese ships.  
The Portuguese state wanted its share of this trade.  

In 1481, a large Portuguese fleet arrived at Edina (now called Elmina).  
They negotiated with Kwamena Ansa, the ruler there.  
The goal was to build a fortress.  
Negotiations were tense. The Portuguese first tried to build on a holy shrine site.  
After talks ended, the fortress at Elmina was built.  
It still stands today.  
This place later became known as the Gold Coast.  
In the 1600s, the Dutch took over the fortress.  
Later, the Dutch and English became the main European traders in Ghana.  

Because trade on the Gold Coast grew, many Akan rulers wanted more trading links.  
The Portuguese built forts at other places along the coast.  
These include Axim and Komenda.  
Most were completed by 1500.  
Later, almost every few miles had a fort.  
Some forts focused on gold trade.  
Others, like Anishan, exported corn, which Europeans also wanted.  
The slave trade did not become the main trade until the 1700s.  

Other West and West-Central African rulers also met Portuguese traders.  
Oba Ozolua of Benin welcomed Portuguese visitors in 1485.  
An Atlantic trading post called Gwatón was founded around 1490.  
Benin first sold malaguetta peppers to the Portuguese.  
But after a sea route to India opened in 1499, pepper demand in Europe fell.  
The Portuguese tried to send enslaved people from Benin to Elmina’s gold traders.  
Oba Ozolua refused this request.  

Over the 1500s, Benin’s contact with Portugal declined.  
By the early 1600s, Benin Obas made new links with Dutch traders.  
Dutch wanted Benin’s cloth.  
Cloth remained Benin’s main export through the 1600s.  
Ambassy cloths were traded regularly to Elmina and as far as Brazil.  
But demand for Benin cloth fell in the late 1600s.  
This was because luxury cloths from India became more common.  
By the 1700s, Benin Obas had to rely on the trade of enslaved persons.  
They did this to keep and rebuild power in Edo and the Benin state.  

Portuguese voyages continued south after Benin.  
They reached the mouth of the Kongo River.  
They made contact with Nzika Nkuwu, the manikongo (king) at Mbanza Kongo, the capital.  

By 1485, Portuguese settled the island of São Tomé.  
Many BaKongo people were taken there as enslaved persons.  
They worked on sugar plantations.  

In 1491, Nzika Nkuwu converted to Christianity.  
He took the name João I.  
This led to stronger links between Kongo, Elmina, and São Tomé.  
Trade moved through these places.  

By the 1510s, traders from Benin were present at the Kongolese port of Mpinda.  
A Portuguese letter from the new manikongo, Afonso I (who ruled 1509–1546), mentions this.  

Therefore, by the 1510s, many different West African peoples and rulers had contact with the Portuguese.  
Some, like Benin and Elmina, also linked further south to Kongo.  
African rulers wanted to expand their trade.  
At times, they sought military support against rivals.  
Benin used Portuguese help in a major battle against Nupe in 1516.  
Civil wars in Jolof and Kongo also saw such requests for aid.

4.  **No complex clauses or parentheses:** All information from original notes is woven into main flow using simple connective words ("This suggests...", "Archaeology has not proven this clearly...").  
5.  **Line breaks between ideas:** Visual separation helps signal topic changes (e.g., moving from Cape Verde to Ghana, then Benin, etc.).  
6.  **Plain language without oversimplification:** Uses common words ("trade," "fort," "ruler") but retains precise terms ("trans-Saharan trade," "manikongo," "malaguetta peppers," "ambassy cloths") as they are essential for accuracy. No meaning is lost or altered.

### West African Diplomacy with Portugal (Early Period)

West African kingdoms built diplomatic ties with Portugal early on.  
Princes from Benin, Jolof, and Kongo often studied or worked in Portugal.  
Some were sent as royal ambassadors to the Portuguese court.  

This continued into the 1600s.  
Kongo sent ambassadors to Dutch Brazil, the Vatican (home of the Catholic Church), and Portugal.  
In the 1650s, Allada also sent ambassadors to the Spanish court.  
Later, Dahomey sent ambassadors five times to Portuguese Brazil and Portugal.  
This happened between 1755 and the 1810s.  
When Brazil became independent from Portugal in 1811, Dahomey was the first state to recognize its independence.  

Portuguese kings also saw these links as diplomatic.  
Under King João II (1481–1495), Portugal sent ambassadors to African courts.  
They went to Benin, Kongo, and the Mali emperor (the Mandimansa).  
One Portuguese envoy tried to reach Timbuktu.  
We do not know if he arrived there.  

Portuguese kings wrote letters to West African rulers.  
They treated them as fellow monarchs.  
Both in Africa and Portugal, kingship was seen as a divine gift.  
This created some common understanding between them.  

Some portraits of these ambassadors survive.  
The most important were painted in Brazil by a Dutch artist (probably Jasper Beckx).  
They show Dom Miguel de Castro.  
He was an ambassador from the Kongo court.  
His king was Garcia II Nkanza a Luquini nzenze atumba.  
Dom Miguel de Castro was sent to the Dutch court in Brazil, likely in 1643.  

Ambassadors had different goals.  
These can be grouped into three main areas:  

1.  **Military Alliances**  
    *Example one:* In 1488, a Jolof prince named Bumi Jeléen came to Portugal.  
    He claimed he was the true ruler of Jolof.  
    His brothers had removed him from the throne.  
    He asked King João II for military help.  
    João II sent a fleet to support him when he returned to Senegal.  
    But Pero Vaz de Cunha, who led the fleet, murdered Bumi Jeléen.  
    Pero Vaz thought Bumi Jeléen might betray them.  
    This was a shameful failure.  
    King João II had many of the plotters executed.  
    Bumi Jeléen’s family and followers moved to Cape Verde, which Portugal controlled then.  

    *Example two:* In the 1640s, Kongo allied with the Dutch against Portugal.  
    The Dutch took Luanda in 1641.  
    Kongo armies fought Portuguese troops at forts Ambaca and Massangano in Angola.  
    Dom Miguel de Castro was sent by the Kongo king to discuss military plans.  
    He wanted to talk about how to remove the Portuguese from West-Central Africa forever.  
    But this alliance failed in 1648. The Dutch and their allies lost.  

2.  **Interest in Christianity**  
    Some African rulers wanted more contact with Christians.  
    Princes from Benin and Kongo studied at Portuguese missions.  
    Interest in Christianity lessened in Benin.  
    But it stayed strong in Kongo.  
    Kongo kings sent repeated requests to the Vatican for more priests and missionaries, well into the 1700s.  
    In the 1670s, over a dozen members of the Ndongo royal family spent years studying in Portuguese monasteries and convents (as new research by historian José Lingna Nafafé shows).  
    Allada also asked Spain for missionaries in the mid-1600s.  
    Their king hoped priests could help stop frequent floods and unpredictable weather.  

3.  **Trade and Money**  
    Trade was often why kings sent ambassadors.  
    Access to Atlantic trade helped rulers get more money.  
    Different types of money were used in West Africa before Europeans arrived.  
    These included:  
    *   Gold, especially on the Niger Bend and in Akan kingdoms (Gold Coast).  
    *   Cowries, used in Benin, Oyò, the Niger Bend, later Hueda and Dahomey.  
    *   Copper rods, used on the Gold Coast and in Calabar.  
    *   Iron bars, used in Senegambia and on the Gold Coast.  
    *   Strips of cloth, used widely in Senegambia, Sierra Leone, parts of the Gold Coast, and Oyò.  

    Atlantic trade increased the total money available.  
    This grew market exchanges.  
    West African rulers hoped to get more currency through deals with European monarchs.  
    More currency meant higher tax income.  
    Higher taxes made their states stronger.  

    In the 1620s, smaller Gold Coast kingdoms sent embassies to the Dutch for trade reasons.  
    Trade was also a clear reason for Allada’s embassies in the 1650s.  
    All five Dahomey embassies to Brazil and Portugal in the late 1700s and early 1800s had commercial aims.  

    By this later time, Dahomey’s royal family knew how to live well in Brazilian and Portuguese capitals.  
    The 1795 embassy is a good example.  
    The two ambassadors first went to Salvador, Brazil.  
    They spent large sums on fine silk, damask clothing, and hats.  
    Portugal paid for these expenses.  
    Later that year, they traveled to Lisbon, Portugal.  
    In Lisbon, they visited the theatre and opera every night.  

West African rulers had goals similar to other kings: military success, religious belief, and trade.  
The Portuguese crown also sent many early embassies.  
But by the 1530s, European presence in West Africa became less formal.  
Small-scale traders took over more direct contact than royal ambassadors.

### European Trading Communities in West Africa: Two Main Types

There were two main types of European trading communities in West Africa.

1.  **Informal communities.**  
    Europeans settled here. They married local women. Together, they formed African families. These families often became important in local trade networks.

2.  **Formal communities.**  
    These grew up in fortified trading posts along the coast. They were called *factories* (from the Portuguese word *feitoria*).  
    Factories were especially found:  
    *   Along the Gold Coast,  
    *   In Hueda,  
    *   Around rivers in Guinea-Bissau and Gambia (especially the Gambia, Casamance, São Domingos, Corubal, Nunez, and Pongo rivers).

The biggest and oldest trading post was Elmina. It was built in the 1480s for gold trade. This shows how important gold trade was at first.  
However, in the 1500s, informal communities were more common than formal ones along many coasts.

Male Portuguese traders went to places like Senegambia, Guinea-Bissau rivers, Sierra Leone, and Benin. There, they married local women.  
These couples often acted as trading intermediaries with local rulers. Why? Because the wife (and their children) could speak both African and European languages well. This helped trade.

One famous trader in Senegambia was Ganagoga in the 16th century.  
His original name was João Ferreira. He married the daughter of the ruler of Fùùta Tòòro (on the Senegal river).  
His new name, *Ganagoga*, meant "he who speaks all the languages" in the Biafada language of Guinea-Bissau. This shows how valuable language skill was.

It seems common for traders to marry daughters of ruling families.  
In the early 17th century, a Dutch Jewish trader had an affair with the daughter of the Buur of Kajoor in Senegal. This caused him problems.

Some historians think these early European settlers also took religious roles.  
Portuguese called settled Europeans *tangomãos* in the 1500s.  
This word came from *tunguma*, a shrine name in Sierra Leone.  
In 1506, a writer said one of the first Portuguese men in Sierra Leone (in the 1480s) officiated at this shrine. He did this after Temni people asked him to.  
*Tangomão* therefore meant: a European who settled in West Africa and adopted local beliefs and practices.

In many informal communities, **African women married to European men ran the trading networks.**  
Why? European men often got sick with malaria and other diseases. They had no resistance to these diseases. Many became very ill. They spent much time in bed. They often died young.  
European women spoke African languages better. They could build trade and community links easily. They managed daily business while their husbands were sick.  
Some historians link this strong role of African women traders to the powerful positions women later held in anti-colonial independence movements (especially in Guinea-Bissau and parts of Nigeria in the 20th century).

A good example is from Guinea-Bissau in the mid-1600s.  
In the factory at Cacheu, the most powerful traders in the 1660s, 1670s, and 1680s were two women: Bibiana Vaz and Crispina Peres.  
Peres was married to a Portuguese trader. He was too ill to work. So she ran their business alone. Her business success made many enemies. She was captured by the Portuguese Inquisition in 1664. They took her to Lisbon. There, she was tried for "fetishism" (seen as a crime against Catholic Christianity).  
Vaz was very powerful too. She kept the Portuguese Governor of Cacheu prisoner inside her house in Farim for 18 months in the 1690s.

These mixed communities followed mostly African practices, not European ones.  
It was important to speak and write European languages well. This helped get good trade terms with Europeans.  
But marriage and inheritance followed local rules—wherever the European had settled.  
This encouraged Portuguese settlers to choose places where inheritance passed through the female line (matrilineal societies).  
    *   In such places (like Guinea-Bissau or Gold Coast), children from a European man and his African wife inherited rights, social status, and property by local law.  
*   Where inheritance passed through the male line (patrilineal societies), these children had no rights to land or status. Why? Because their fathers were Europeans, born with no rights in that society.  
    *   An example: Senegambia. Very few European men settled there after 1550s.

Informal communities focused on trade. They helped African rulers expand trade links. They negotiated with short-stop European ships to get the best prices. Some families kept ties to Europe, sending children to study in Europe into the 1700s. They became rich coastal merchants.  
Most informal communities fully joined African society by this time. Their male European ancestors had first been guests of African kings.

As noted, informal settlements were most common in the 1500s.  
But by the end of the 1500s and early 1600s, fortified European trading posts became more common—especially on Gold Coast and in Hueda.  
In Casamance and Guinea-Bissau, factories like Cacheu (built 1589), Ziguinchor (1645), and Bissau (1687) were established.  
The fort at James Island (Gambia estuary) was built in 1651.  
Along Gold Coast, the Dutch built more castles: Cape Coast (started 1610, expanded 1652), Sekondi (1642), plus Axim and Elmina already mentioned.

The huge growth of the Atlantic slave trade in the late 1600s increased this formal community model.  
Factories at Offra (Allada port, built 1660) and Hueda were fortified.  
By the mid-1700s, these formal European communities were more important than earlier informal ones. By then, most members of informal communities had fully integrated into their host African societies.

Although protected by military force, formal trading posts relied heavily on African intermediaries for trade.  
Military captains in the forts often took part in royal ceremonies of the local African state (as happened in Dahomey).  
They also sent gifts for funeral rites of important locals. Doing this meant they had to take part in local religious practices linked to funerals.

These formal communities around fortified posts were different from informal ones.  
The military presence was key.  
European traders rented land for their posts, but they acted as occupants too—not just tenants.  
They had armed militias. They often allied with one local ruler. This could cause problems between European groups and rulers.  
By the 1700s, guns were a major import from Atlantic trade to Africa. This changed earlier times when copper, iron, and cloth were also important trades.

European officials in forts often married African women. Their children grew up around the forts. Many became traders later. Why? Their dual heritage gave them access to both their African and European parents' worlds.  
Some of these families became important in local politics. This shows a link to earlier informal communities.

However, by the 1700s, slavery and military presence made formal communities very different in key ways from earlier informal ones.

### Europeans and Early Trade with Africa (Clear & Accessible Version)

Europeans came to Africa mainly to trade. This was their main reason for coming. Most expected a short stay and to make money. Some stayed longer. They formed families within African communities. But even then, trade remained very important.

African rulers saw many opportunities in trade. In the first two centuries, they wanted materials used as money. Cloth was one of the largest imports. It came from India and Europe. Early 17th-century Dutch ships to Senegambia often carried only cloth. Cloth stayed important through the 18th and 19th centuries. The French imported a blue indigo cloth (*pièce de guinée*) made near Pondichéry, India. They brought it to Senegambia. It was used as money along the Upper Senegal River for many years.

Cloth acted as money in Senegambia. It also acted as money in parts of Angola and on the Gold Coast. Copper was a major import too. Especially to Benin and the Gold Coast. Iron bars were important here as well. In Senegambia and the Gold Coast, iron bars had to have a mark from an European company. For example, OWIC (Dutch West Indian Company) or RAC (English Royal African Company). Without this mark, African traders gave them less value. Cowries came from the Maldives to Benin as early as 1505.
