### West Africa in the 17th Century: Climate and Trade Changes

The first half of the 17th century brought many changes to West Africa. These changes were important for the region. They were also part of global changes happening at the same time. Wars and revolutions occurred in places like China, Europe, and Africa during this time.

There were two main reasons for these changes.  
1.  Environmental pressures from a "mini ice age." This peak was around 1640.  
2.  Political competition because of the growing capitalist world system.  

**Reason 1: The Mini Ice Age and Its Effects**  
The mini ice age was a period of cooler global temperatures. It started in the 1570s. This cooling caused climate problems. In Africa, droughts happened in Angola from around 1600. Droughts also hit Senegambia from around 1640. Floods occurred in Yoruba-speaking areas of Nigeria and Benin in the early 17th century. Heavy snows fell in Morocco. When the King of Allada sent ambassadors to Spain in the 1650s, he mentioned severe storms in Allada as a reason for his visit.

Cooler temperatures affected other parts of the world too. Harvests of wheat and other crops failed badly. Food prices rose sharply. The coldest years around 1640 coincided with major revolutions. In China, a civil war began that overthrew the Ming dynasty. In Europe, Portugal declared independence from Spain in 1640, starting a civil war lasting until 1668. England’s civil war began in 1641; the King was deposed and executed. France also faced serious conflict during this time.

Scientists have different ideas about why temperatures fell and political crises happened. Some European historians pointed to sun patterns. However, archaeologists in Colombia offer another explanation. The European conquest of the Americas in the 1500s caused a huge drop in the indigenous population. Recent estimates suggest 90% of Native Americans died from disease and war. This was perhaps 10-15% of the entire world population at that time.

The large loss of indigenous people led to two main environmental changes:  
(a) Forests grew over abandoned settlements and farmland because fewer people were farming.  
(b) There was less forest burning for farming or clearing land, so less carbon dioxide entered the air from fires.  

According to the Colombian archaeologists, growing forests absorbed more carbon dioxide from the air. Less fire also meant less new carbon dioxide. Together, this caused global temperatures to fall. This matches modern understanding: lower carbon emissions and more forest absorption can cool the climate (the opposite of today’s main warming cause).

**Reason 2: Political Competition and Trade**  
As trade and the power of controlling trade grew, political competition increased. In West Africa, building good trading relationships with European partners became very important. States that did this often prospered. However, there could also be costs. Large kingdoms like Jolof and Kongo saw their coastal areas become stronger. These areas broke away from central control. This happened in Jolof’s Kajoor region in the 1550s. It happened in Kongo’s Nsoyo region in the early 17th century. At the same time, rival African rulers tried to open their own trading stations. They competed fiercely for the best access to international trade. This created conflict between African states. It also increased demand for European trade goods. As a result, many fortified trading posts were built along the Gold Coast, and along the coasts of Hueda and Allada in the second half of the 17th century.

European traders also competed strongly with each other for access to African trade. It is important to note that although European nations fought hard to get the best trade, they did not usually fight direct military battles against each other *in Africa* during this time. Wars between Europeans happened in Europe itself. In Africa, European traders worked within a shared system of competition and cooperation. By the second half of the 17th century, Danish, Dutch, English, French, and German trading companies all tried to establish trade posts in West Africa. They brought fashionable goods. They also negotiated with each other to exchange what they had, aiming to build the best overall "assortment" of trade items.

This competition between European traders gave African rulers some advantages. Rulers could often get better deals by playing one European company against another. But it also meant African rulers had to meet traders' demands. If they did not, traders would leave to find captives, ivory, or gold elsewhere. Over time, African rulers and European traders became more dependent on each other. The increasingly fragile environment—in West Africa and globally—caused frequent food and resource shortages. These shortages often led to conflict between groups.

**Reparations: Seeking Fair Compensation After Harm**

Many societies around the world have experienced harm by more powerful groups or classes. This can include colonialism, the Holocaust during World War II, and the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade (TAST). When people free themselves from such harmful situations, they often ask for reparations. Reparations mean fair payment or help to make up for past wrongs.

This payment can be money, resources, or other support. One well-known and discussed case is reparations for slavery in Africa. People argue that descendants of Africans enslaved during the TAST should receive compensation.

The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade moved many Africans to the Americas (the New World). European traders treated people as trade goods, not like gold or ivory. They forced Africans across the Atlantic Ocean after Europeans found the Americas. The goal was to use them for hard labor on plantations.

This trade badly hurt African communities at home and among descendants in the diaspora. Enslaved people were captured in wars, kidnapped, or sold in markets. They suffered terribly during the Middle Passage (the ocean journey), on plantations, and after slavery ended due to lasting trauma.

Because of these deep injustices against enslaved people and their descendants in the Americas, African Americans and people in Caribbean communities are increasingly calling for reparations. They believe fair compensation is needed.

### Christianity and Missions in West Africa: An Introduction (Dyslexia-Friendly Version)

**This chapter focuses on West Africa. We look at how Christianity and Western-style education changed life, values, and attitudes there.**

Many Europeans felt Christians had a duty to help African peoples. They believed Africans needed moral and spiritual renewal. Ending the slave trade also made many Europeans care more about Africa. This concern helped start more mission work.

Mission work brought several forces to Africa:  
*   New trade (not slavery, called "legitimate commerce").  
*   Christianity.  
*   Ideas of European civilization.  
*   Colonial rule.  

The main goal was spreading Christianity and helping Africans spiritually. This work had real costs. Many young missionaries died from the hot, wet tropical climate. In West Africa, moving inland to preach faced challenges. At the same time, Islam was growing stronger in the south. This made it harder for Christian missions to expand deep into the continent. Early mission efforts often met indifference from local people. Success came first on coasts where mixed-race (mulatto) communities and European traders lived.

The first Europeans arrived at West Africa’s coast at the end of the 1400s. For many years, they focused on the slave trade, not teaching Christianity. By the start of the 1800s, churches in Europe began sending missionaries systematically.  
*   Anglicans, Methodists, and Baptists worked in Sierra Leone.  
*   Presbyterians started missions in Nigeria.  
*   Methodists also began work in Ghana, The Gambia, and Dahomey.  
*   Later, Afro-Brazilians (people of African descent from Brazil) brought Catholicism back to Benin and Nigeria.

A new phase began in 1787. Black Christians from Nova Scotia settled in Sierra Leone. Also, from 1799, missionaries began moving inland from Cape Town (South Africa), led by J.T. van der Kemp. New missionary groups started work across Africa: the LMS, CMS, Holy Ghost Fathers, White Fathers, and others.

The CMS (Church Missionary Society) began in freed-slave villages in Sierra Leone in 1804. Methodists started there in 1811. Early successes included Freetown and nearby villages. Other early success areas were:  
*   The Liberian coast, where African Americans and freed slaves converted.  
*   French trading posts like Grand Bassam (Ivory Coast), Assinie, and Libreville (Gabon).

Before the last quarter of the 1800s, Europeans rarely went deep into Africa’s interior. Most stayed near coasts or in established trading posts. The Evangelical Revival (a religious movement) starting at the end of the 1700s brought many new missionaries to Africa. Their work laid the first strong foundations for Christianity across sub-Saharan Africa.

In the later 1800s, Catholic priests focused heavily on the African interior. From 1867 until his death in November 1892, Cardinal Lavigerie planned to plant churches throughout Africa south of the Sahara Desert.

It is important to remember:  
*   Modern Christian mission history in Africa really began in the late 1700s.  
*   Catholics were in parts of Africa earlier, during the first centuries of Christianity—especially with early Portuguese voyages.  
*   Because of this earlier presence, the big wave of missions starting in the late 1800s is often seen as a continuation or renewal, not a completely new beginning.  
*   The rise of new missionary groups in Europe in the late 1700s directly led to more African missions. For example:  
    *   The Baptist Missionary Society formed on 2 October 1792.  
    *   The London Missionary Society (interdenominational) started in 1795.  
    *   The British and Foreign Bible Society began in 1804, with the job of translating and printing Bibles.  
*   At first, most missionaries were English-speaking Protestants.  
*   Later, in the 1820s and 1830s, missionaries from Germany, Switzerland, and France also went to Africa.  
*   Related mission groups also formed in Scandinavia, Holland, and the United States.

West Africa owes a great debt to Christian missionaries. They did more than bring a new religion that changed millions of lives. They also started Western-style schools and education systems used across West Africa today.

The Portuguese were the first Europeans to bring Christianity to West Africa. But they left the coast by the mid-1600s. After they left, Christianity survived only in Upper Guinea. A bishop based on the Cape Verde Islands served churches there and on the mainland. Christianity was not truly established across West Africa until the 1800s.

**In this chapter, we examine how Christianity and Western education shaped West African values, attitudes, and daily life.**

This inspired men and women to start religious societies. Their goal was to travel to Africa and other lands.  

These societies had three main purposes:  
1.  To share the message of the Gospel.  
2.  To provide social services for local people.  
3.  To help stop slavery and the slave trade.  

The groups saw these actions as Europe’s repair for long-term harm done to Africans.  
This harm came especially from the Trans-Atlantic slave trade over many centuries.  

Several Protestant evangelical societies began in Great Britain:  
*   The Baptist Missionary Society.  
*   The Church Missionary Society for the Propagation of the Gospel.  
*   The Wesleyan Missionary Society.  
*   The Presbyterian Missionary Society of the Church of Scotland.  

Other European countries also formed similar societies. These included:  
*   The Basel Missionary Society in Switzerland.  
*   The Breman Mission in Germany.  

Missionary groups were founded in the Americas too. These were:  
*   The Baptist Missionary Board.  
*   The Nova Scotian Methodists.  
The Nova Scotian Methodists worked mainly with the Maroons. Many Maroons settled in Liberia.  

At the same time, evangelical movements spread in West Africa.  
Roman Catholic missionary efforts also grew in Europe.  
They were supported by the Vatican’s Propagation of the Faith office.  
Its Cardinal Secretary later became Pope Gregory XVI.  

Many Roman Catholic missionary societies were created because of this:  
*   The Congregation of the Holy Ghost (often called the Holy Ghost Fathers).  
*   The Society of African Missions (SMA).  
*   The Society of Missionaries of Africa. People usually called them the White Fathers. They wore white, robe-like clothing similar to some Muslim styles.  
*   The Society of the Divine Word (SVD), short for its Latin name.

chapter_key: Establishment of Christian Churches In Nigeria
text:
Here is a revised version focusing on dyslexia accessibility and readability, using clear, short sentences, consistent structure, precise wording, and avoiding complex phrasing or ambiguous terms. All facts and meanings from the original text are preserved:

**Christianity Comes to Nigeria: Early Missionaries (Dyslexia-Friendly Version)**

Portuguese traders came to Nigeria long ago. Catholic priests started missionary stations in Benin and nearby places.  
But Christianity was not firmly established in Nigeria until the 1800s (nineteenth century).  

It began with Yoruba people. These were freed slaves. They had become Christian while in Sierra Leone. The British Royal Navy rescued them from slave ships. Between 1839 and 1845, they returned home to Nigeria.  
Church Missionary Society (CMS) pastors visited their communities. This happened in Abeokuta and other towns.  
One of the first missionaries was Rev. Henry Townsend. He went from Sierra Leone to Badagry in 1842. Rev. Ajayi Crowther traveled with him.  

The pioneer missionaries had success. CMS churches became strong in many important towns:  
*   Abeokuta: established in 1846  
*   Lagos: established in 1851  
*   Ibadan: established in 1853  
*   Oyo: established in 1856  

Later, CMS started churches in south-eastern Nigeria. Key places were Bonny and Brass.  
Bishop Ajayi Crowther worked hard there. He was helped by Rev. J.C. Taylor, an Igbo freed slave. Their work can still be seen today in southern Nigeria.  

Other missionary groups also started work in Nigeria:  
*   **Baptist missionaries:** They began from Ogbomosho in 1855. Thomas Bowen, an American evangelist, led them.  
*   **Church of Scotland (Presbyterian):** Rev. Hope Waddell started work in Calabar in 1846. Later, Rev. Hugh Goldie and William Anderson joined him.  
*   **Mary Slessor:** She arrived in Nigeria in 1876. She worked as a missionary nurse for many years. She successfully stopped the killing of twins in the areas she served.  

The story of Christianity in Nigeria must include Father Berghero. He was an Italian Roman Catholic priest. He worked from Whydah (in today’s Benin, formerly Dahomey). In 1860, he visited Abeokuta and Lagos. Freed Catholic slaves from Brazil welcomed him there.  
A permanent Catholic station opened in Lagos in 1868. Soon after, stations were started at Lokoja, Abeokuta, and Ibadan.  
Within ten years of his visit, the Roman Catholic Church in Nigeria was strong enough to no longer be under the administration from Dahomey.  

By 1885, Catholicism had spread further inland. Father Joseph Lutz began work around Onitsha in 1886. He preached the gospel in many parts of present-day Imo and Anambra States.  
Bishop Shanahan, an Irishman, was also important in this area.  

Lokoja had a small CMS station as early as 1858.  
But missionaries did not enter Hausaland (the northern region) until 1889. Hausaland was mostly Muslim at that time.  
For many years, converts were mainly:  
*   People of southern Nigerian origin living in the north.  
*   The large non-Muslim population already in the north.

**Revised Chapter: Europe, West Africa, and Early Portuguese Voyages**

Europe in the 14th century was in a bad way.  
The Plague spread between 1346 and 1353.  
It is estimated that this Plague killed 30 to 50 percent of people living in Europe.  

Some archaeologists think the Plague also affected West African populations.  
Archaeologist Gérard Chouin has argued strongly for this idea.  
Other archaeologists challenge this evidence.  
This remains an interesting but debated hypothesis.  

After the Plague, many Europeans died.  
The population of Europe dropped sharply.  
This caused big problems in European countries like Portugal.  
Portugal lost more than half its workers.  
With fewer workers, much farmland was not used anymore.  
Forest and plants grew on empty fields.  

An early record from Portugal in 1471 tells us something important.  
It comes from the Portuguese parliament at Évora.  
This record says African labourers helped clear wastelands in Portugal.  
This shows there was a strong shortage of workers after the Plague.  
It also shows that African workers were used to help fix this problem.  

Many nobles in Portugal lost their farm workers (serfs).  
Serfs were workers who had to stay on a noble's land.  
The loss of workers led to civil wars in Portugal in the 1380s.  
There was not enough wheat to make bread.  
The value of Portuguese money (the escudo) became very high quickly.  
This is called high inflation.  

These problems made Portugal interested in Morocco.  
Morocco had fertile land and grew a lot of wheat.  
Portuguese sailors also hoped to find gold by sailing along the West African coast.  
They wanted to protect their own money supply from losing value.  
Finding gold could help with this goal.  

At the same time, many states in West Africa in the 15th century were growing stronger.  
The Mossi kingdom began in Burkina Faso in the 15th century.  
Kano became a major power.  
The Songhay empire grew strong and took over the Mali Empire.  

Much of this growth came from gold.  
Gold was produced in large amounts in Akan states like Ghana.  
There was so much gold that traders going across the Sahara sometimes brought back no goods to sell at Kano.  
They would return empty-handed.  
This is what the early 16th-century Muslim traveller Leo Africanus wrote about.  

Portuguese leaders knew about West Africa from several sources.  
One source was the Catalan Atlas, made around 1375.  
This map was drawn by Abraham Cresques, a Jewish man from Majorca.  
The atlas showed Mali and its gold production in detail.  

The atlas also showed good trade routes between Spain and West Africa across the Sahara.  
Jewish traders often used these routes.  
These traders told people in Spain and Portugal about West Africa.  
There were Jewish communities living in Saharan settlements like Tuat.  
After riots against Jews in Spain in 1391, more Jews moved to Morocco.  
In Morocco, they worked in carpet and textile trade with the Mali Empire.  

Because of these sources, Portuguese leaders wanted to connect with West African gold producers.  
Portugal also had a large Jewish population who could help.  
Leaders hoped to meet a Christian king they called Prester John.  
They believed he lived somewhere in Africa.  
They wanted an alliance with him against the growing Islamic Ottoman Empire.  
They also hoped to get some of West Africa's gold for themselves.  
Prester John probably meant the Christian King of Ethiopia, but this was not known at the time.  

All these reasons helped shape Portuguese voyages to West Africa.  
These reasons led them to arrive at the Senegal River in 1442.

European explorers changed life in the Americas.

Miguel de Cervantes wrote it.  
The book was published in two parts: 1605 and later in 1618.  

*Don Quixote* tells a story about a gentleperson (hidalgo).  
He reads many old tales about knights.  
Because of these stories, he cannot always tell real things from imagined ones.

He wants to bring back knightly behavior.  
He sets out to fight what he thinks are Spain's enemies.

Here is a revised version focusing on dyslexia accessibility and readability. It uses short sentences, simple words, active voice, concrete phrasing, and avoids complex structures or ambiguous terms. All facts and meanings from the original are preserved:

**Original Key Facts Preserved:**
*   English promoters wrote about colony benefits (resources, markets, spreading Protestantism), many never went themselves.
*   Actual migrants had different goals: commercial in Chesapeake (Virginia/Maryland), religious in New England.
*   Chesapeake focused on tobacco farming; thousands of young unmarried men (and some women) came for this.
*   New England settlers were mainly Puritans, motivated by religion, often bringing families, seeking a "new Israel" to reform Protestantism and counter Catholicism.
*   New England built church-centered towns with local congregation decisions; this led to the Congregational Church.
*   Historians link early North/South differences to Chesapeake vs. New England colony contrasts.
*   Root causes were English domestic issues: Church of England demanded conformity, Puritans wanted reform; by 1620s, Puritans seen as threats.
*   By 1640, New England had ~25,000 people; loyal Church members often went to Virginia for money.
*   English Civil War (1640s) pitted Royalists/Church supporters vs. Parliamentarians (Puritan reformers).
*   Parliament executed Charles I in 1649; England became a republic in the 1950s.
*   Colonists followed events closely: some Puritans returned to England to fight; Chesapeake colonists feared Puritan rule.
*   English turmoil made imperial oversight hard, helping the two regions develop different cultures.

---

**Revised Chapter (Dyslexia-Accessible & Readable)**

Some English people who stayed in England wrote about North America. They said English settlers would find good food and resources there. These writers hoped to make money. They wanted raw materials from the colonies. They also wanted new places to sell English goods. Spreading Protestantism was another goal for them.

But the English people who actually traveled to America had different reasons. In the Chesapeake Bay area, settlers started Virginia and Maryland. Their main aim was business. Early Virginians at Jamestown first looked for gold. But they and Maryland settlers soon learned tobacco grew well there. Growing tobacco was the surest way to earn money.

Thousands of young English men came to work in the tobacco fields. Many were unmarried, unemployed, or eager for change. A smaller number of English women also went. They hoped for a better life on the tobacco farms of Virginia and Maryland.

A very different group went to New England. They faced cold weather and rocky ground. Their main reason was religion. Most were Puritans. Many Puritan families crossed the ocean together. They often followed their own church ministers. They dreamed of building a new community in America. This place would follow reformed Protestant ideas strictly. They wanted it to be a good example for all Christians. They also saw it as a way to oppose what they called the Catholic danger.

While people in Virginia and Maryland worked on tobacco fields, New Englanders built towns around churches. In New England, each town’s congregation decided its own rules. This church system became known as the Congregational Church. It started with the Puritan settlers.

Many historians think the early differences between the North and South in the United States began here. The big divide was between the Chesapeake colonies and New England.

These colony differences came from problems inside England itself. Starting in the early 1600s, the official English church – the Church of England (made law in the 1530s) – required people to follow its rules exactly. Puritans wanted more changes to the church. By the 1620s, leaders of the Church of England saw leading Puritan preachers and their followers as dangerous. They thought Puritans threatened national safety because they opposed church power. As church rules became stricter, many Puritans decided to move to New England.

By 1640, about twenty-five thousand people lived in New England. Meanwhile, many loyal members of the Church of England – who often laughed at or mocked Puritans in England and in America – chose to go to Virginia for work and money.

Big trouble began in England in the 1640s. A civil war started. One side supported King Charles I and the Church of England. The other side supported Parliament. This second side included many Puritan reformers and their supporters. In 1649, Parliament defeated the king’s forces. Parliament then executed King Charles I. This was a very unusual event.

In the 1650s, England had no king. It was a republic for a short time. English colonists in America paid close attention to these events. Some Puritans who were in New England returned home. They wanted to join the fight against the king and the national church. Other English people living in Virginia and other colonies were very worried. They feared the destruction and chaos that Parliament’s Puritan leaders seemed to cause in England. The big fighting in England made it hard for English officials to control the Chesapeake and New England colonies. Because of this, the two regions slowly grew to have different ways of life and different cultures.

**Slavery in the English Colonies: Early Changes**

The shift from indentured servitude to slavery started first in the West Indies.  
Barbados was colonized by England in the 1620s.  
At first, planters grew tobacco as their main crop.  
By the 1640s, they switched to sugarcane.  
They began using more people from Africa who were enslaved.  

In 1655, England took control of Jamaica from Spain.  
Jamaica quickly became a major sugar island.  
It relied entirely on forced labor for England’s growing empire.  

Slavery grew slower in the Chesapeake colonies (Virginia and Maryland).  
But by the end of the 1600s, both used chattel slavery as their main labor force.  
Chattel slavery legally treated Africans as property, not people.  
They used enslaved people to grow tobacco.  
Colonists also enslaved Native peoples in this region.  

**Early Arrivals in Virginia (1619)**  
Slavery did not exist in England at this time.  
It was not yet a formal system in colonial America when the first Africans arrived in Virginia in 1619.  
Many Africans worked as servants, like White people.  
Some could own their own land.  
Some who converted to Christianity became free landowners.  
Some even had White servants of their own.  

The status of Africans in the Chesapeake changed toward enslavement in the last decades of the 1600s.  

**Bacon’s Rebellion (1675–1676)**  
This rebellion helped speed up the move to African slavery in Virginia and Maryland.  
It was called Bacon’s Rebellion after Nathaniel Bacon.  
Bacon arrived in Virginia in 1674.  
He was a young, wealthy Englishman.  
He first had a friendly relationship with Governor William Berkeley.  
But Bacon felt excluded from the governor’s important circle.  
Bacon wanted land on Virginia’s frontier.  
The governor refused, fearing war with nearby Native tribes.  

Many former indentured servants joined Bacon.  
They believed the governor limited their chances for land and wealth.  
They thought he did not do enough to clear land from Native Americans.  
Bacon’s followers felt the governor did not protect settlers well enough.  
They also strongly disliked his peace treaties with local Native peoples.  
Bacon and his group saw all Native peoples as obstacles to getting land.  
They wanted to remove them completely—a policy of extermination.  

War broke out in 1675.  
Susquehannock warriors attacked frontier settlements.  
They killed English planters and destroyed farms, including one owned by Bacon.  

In 1676, Bacon and other Virginians attacked Susquehannock people without the governor’s order.  
When Berkeley ordered Bacon’s arrest, Bacon led his followers to Jamestown.  
They forced the governor to flee to Virginia’s eastern shore.  
Then they burned parts of Jamestown.  

A civil war followed between supporters of the governor and supporters of Bacon.  
News of the rebellion reached England.  
King Charles II sent royal troops and commissioners to restore order.  
By late 1676, those loyal to the governor won.  
They executed several rebel leaders.  
Bacon himself escaped execution but died soon after from dysentery.  

The rebellion ended in 1676.  
But deep divisions remained among Virginians about Native lands and power.  

**How Bacon’s Rebellion Changed Slavery**  
This event helped create a system of racial slavery in the Chesapeake.  
At that time, indentured servants were the main workers.  
Wealthy White people worried about this large group of workers.  
They feared the freedom servants had.  
They also worried about Black and White servants working together during the rebellion.  

Replacing indentured servitude with African slavery reduced these fears.  
It lessened reliance on White indentured servants, who often felt dissatisfied.  
It created a strict system where race defined a person’s labor status.  
Movement for enslaved people was tightly controlled.  
It also made it harder for Black and White workers to unite again.  
Racial slavery even helped ease tensions between rich and poor White people.  
Now, many poor Whites felt part of a “superior” racial group.  

**New Laws After the Rebellion**  
Colonial laws had already made slavery legal before Bacon’s Rebellion.  
But new laws passed right after it took away more freedom for Black people.  
These laws built the foundation for full racial slavery.  

In 1680, Virginia passed a law with strict rules:  
* Free Black people and enslaved people could not carry weapons.  
* Black people could not gather in large groups.  
* Harsh punishments were set for enslaved people who hurt Christians or tried to escape.  

Two years later, in 1682, another Virginia law stated clearly:  
All Africans brought to the colony would be enslaved for life.  

These changes did two things:  
First, they helped planters get enough workers for tobacco farms.  
Second, they made English leaders feel safer.  
They thought it reduced the risk of future uprisings.  
It also lessened class tensions between rich and poor White people.

    *   White people who worked for others were called "Servants." Some had contracts ("Indentures") stating how long they would work (often until age 24). Others followed local custom, usually working until age 21 if under 19 when first claimed, or 5 years if older than 19.

    Enslaved people worked for life, not for a set number of years like some White servants. This is why they were named "Slaves" – their servitude lasted their whole life.

3.  **Work Done:**  
    Both enslaved people and White male servants did the same field work: tilling soil, manuring fields, sowing and planting crops like tobacco and corn.

**New England Colony: Early Foundations (1600s)**

The English colonized two main areas in the first half of the 1600s. One was New England. It was different from the tobacco colonies in Virginia and Maryland. Those started for money. New England started with religion.

In the 1630s, many Puritan families settled in New England. They had wanted church changes in England since the 1580s. These reformers followed John Calvin’s Protestant ideas. They were called Puritans. They wanted to remove what they saw as un-Biblical practices from the Church of England, especially old Catholic traditions.

Many early New England leaders were trained ministers. They studied at Cambridge or Oxford. But because they questioned church rules, the king and his officials blocked their jobs. They could not work as clergy in England. Other Puritan leaders, like John Winthrop (first governor of Massachusetts Bay Colony), were wealthy landowners. Most Puritans who left England did not want general religious freedom. They wanted to practice *their own* religion without being punished. New England let them live as they believed the Bible required. They aimed to build a strict Protestant society, which they called a "new English Israel."

Puritan beliefs caused big splits in England. They opposed popular Sunday activities. For example, they spoke against bear-baiting: dogs attacking a chained bear, often done on Sundays when people had free time. In the era of Shakespeare’s plays, Puritans wanted to close theaters. They saw playhouses as immoral places. The Bible itself became part of the conflict with King James I. Soon after becoming king, he ordered a new Bible translation. This was to reduce reliance on the Geneva Bible (which followed Calvin and stressed God’s authority over kings). The King James Version, printed in 1611, instead highlighted the king’s divine right.

By the 1620s and 1630s, tensions grew. The official church banned Puritan ministers from preaching. Church leaders saw Puritans as a threat to national security. Their demands for religious, social, and cultural change challenged the king’s power. Many unwilling to follow the Church of England left England. But not all Puritans agreed. **The Glorious Revolution & The 1689 Bill of Rights**  
The Glorious Revolution changed England. It created a nation where the king’s power was limited. It also gave protections to English people.  

In October 1689, William and Mary became king and queen. That same year, Parliament passed the 1689 Bill of Rights. This law made Britain a constitutional monarchy.  

The Bill of Rights said Parliament must be independent from the king. It protected key rights for Parliament. These include:  
* Freedom to speak in Parliament.  
* The right to hold regular elections.  
* The right to ask the king for changes (petition).  

The Bill of Rights also gave rights to all English people. These include:  
* The right to a trial by jury.  
* The right to habeas corpus. This means authorities must bring an imprisoned person before a court. They must show why that person is in jail.  

**John Locke and His Ideas**  
John Locke (1632–1704) was a doctor and teacher. He had lived in exile in Holland during King James II’s rule. After the Glorious Revolution, he returned to England.  

In 1690, Locke published *Two Treatises of Government*. In it, he argued that government is an agreement between leaders and the people (a social contract). He said representative government exists to protect three things: life, liberty, and property.  

Locke rejected the idea of "divine right of kings." This belief says kings get their power directly from God and cannot be questioned. Instead, Locke supported a strong Parliament with a limited king.  

Locke’s ideas had a big impact later. Colonists in America used his thoughts when building their own government. His work showed that representation—having people choose their leaders—is very important for good government.

**Founding Georgia: Oglethorpe's Plan and Its Changes**

Enlightenment ideas had wide influence in the 1730s. They helped start a new colony. James Oglethorpe was a member of Parliament. He cared about social reform. He saw how bad debtors' prison was. He also saw poor former debtors struggling on London streets. Oglethorpe asked King George II for permission to start a new colony. The king agreed. He knew a British colony could protect South Carolina from Spanish Florida. In 1732, the king gave Oglethorpe and 20 others a charter to found Georgia.

Oglethorpe led the first settlers to Georgia in 1733. They sailed on the ship *Anne*. There were 113 people in this first group. Over the next ten years, Parliament paid for more settlers to move there. About 2,500 people came. This made Georgia unusual: it was the only colony fully funded by the British government.

Oglethorpe had a clear plan for Georgia. He wanted it to follow Enlightenment ideas. He saw it as a place for England’s "worthy poor" to begin a new life. To help them start farming, Oglethorpe gave each new male settler:
*   50 acres of land
*   Tools
*   Enough food and supplies for one year
His plan for Savannah aimed for fairness. He wanted all men treated equally. He hoped Georgia would be a good example of farming that supports everyone.

Oglethorpe’s rules banned alcohol and slavery at first. However, new colonists who came from other places—especially South Carolina—did not follow these bans. Many settlers already used enslaved people or accepted alcohol. Slowly, the colony changed. By the 1750s, Georgia was growing large amounts of rice. Enslaved people did most of the hard work to grow and harvest this rice.

This means: Although Oglethorpe began Georgia with Enlightenment ideals—helping poor people and banning slavery—the colony’s early vision did not last. Slavery became common in Georgia, especially for rice farming, by the 1750s.

1. Parliament has supreme power over the colonies.  
2. Any laws the colonies pass must follow Parliament's rules.  
3. If colonial laws go against Parliament, they are not valid.

Women in colonial America had many important home duties. They cared for children and managed the household. The war for independence made their work harder. In some ways, it also kept their roles clear.

Husbands and sons left home to fight. Women then had more to do at home. They also had to help the army directly. Women produced items for the war effort. These included clothing and food. They kept their own homes running while doing this.

Women were often asked to give food and shelter to soldiers. They also nursed wounded men after battles.

The Revolution did open new public roles for some women. An informal group called the Daughters of Liberty formed around 1765. They worked hard to support the war effort against British taxes.

Esther DeBerdt Reed lived in Philadelphia. Her husband was Governor Joseph Reed. She started the Ladies Association of Philadelphia. This group raised money for the Continental Army. They bought supplies the soldiers needed.

In 1780, Esther wrote a letter to other women. She said: *"The time has come to show the same feelings we had at the start of the Revolution. Then, we stopped using tea, even though we liked it, because it came from our enemies. We showed them we thought basic needs were more important than comforts when our freedom was at stake. Our hard-working hands spun flax and made linen for the soldiers' use. When we were exiles or fugitives, we faced all the hardships of war with courage."*

**Early Views on Society and Government After the Revolution**

The American Revolution ended British rule in the United States.  
Some people supported the new 1787 Constitution. They were called Federalists.  

Federalists had views about society that came from Britain.  
They believed in clear social ranks.  

At first, Federalists did not form a political party.  
But they shared some main ideas.  

One idea: only people who owned property could take part in politics.  
This meant many citizens could not vote or hold office.  

Federalists did not think the Revolution changed traditional roles.  
They believed social roles between men and women stayed the same.  
They believed social roles between White people and other groups stayed the same.  

Federalists thought there were clear differences in rank and intelligence.  
To them, the idea that all people were equal seemed unreasonable.  

Women, Black people, and Native peoples, they argued, had lower status.  
They said these groups were secondary to White male citizens.  
They feared trying to force equality would harm the new republic.  

Federalists thought the United States was created as a republic, not a democracy.  

The people who wrote the Constitution held leading positions in the new government.  
Most members of the first national government were Federalists.  

George Washington became president. He chose his first cabinet carefully.  
Alexander Hamilton, a leading Federalist, became Secretary of the Treasury.  
Thomas Jefferson became Secretary of State.  
Henry Knox, who fought with Washington in the Revolution, became Secretary of War.  
Edmond Randolph, a Virginia delegate at the Constitutional Convention, became Attorney General.  

In July 1789, Congress passed the Judiciary Act.  
This law created a Supreme Court with six justices.  
All justices strongly supported the new national government.  

Congress passed its first major law in 1789: the Tariff Act.  
This law placed a tax on imported goods.  
The goal was to raise money for the country’s economy.  
Nationalists supported this. They wanted a strong federal government.  
They had tried similar laws during the Confederation years of the 1780s, without success.  

Congress also passed another rule about foreign ships.  
Ships from other countries paying to enter American ports had to pay fifty cents per ton.  
This tax was based on cargo weight, not ship size.  
The rule gave American ships and goods a commercial advantage.

But there was agreement on one thing: who could be a citizen.

The 1790 Naturalization Act set this rule clearly. To become a U.S. citizen, an immigrant had to be a "free White person." They also had to have "good character."

This law left out many groups. It excluded enslaved people. It excluded free Black people. It excluded Native people. It excluded Asian people.

Because of this law, the United States began as a republic where only White men held full citizenship rights in practice.

Voting rights were also limited. Most state constitutions said only men who owned property or paid taxes could vote.

Women could not vote in most places. One exception was New Jersey. In 1776, New Jersey's constitution allowed unmarried women to vote. But only if they owned property worth £50.

Federalists and Democratic-Republicans both tried to get votes from these New Jersey women who qualified.

### Work Life Before and During Factories (Dyslexia-Accessible Version)

**Work before factories was different.**  
Farmers and skilled artisans controlled their own work pace. They decided when to do each task. If a farmer wanted to fix his fence on Thursday instead of Wednesday, he could do it then. If an artisan felt like stopping for the afternoon, he could take a break. Workers often talked together during the day. In some places, journeymen (traveling skilled workers) were even promised alcohol as part of their pay. One person might read a book or newspaper aloud to the group. When the weather was warm, doors and windows stayed open. Work stopped when it became too dark to see clearly.

**Work in factories changed a lot.**  
Factory workers had to arrive at a set time, usually very early in the morning. They were expected to work all day until their shift ended. Workers could not leave when they felt tired. Breaks only happened at specific times. If someone arrived late, pay was taken away. Being just 5 minutes late could mean losing several hours of wages. Repeated lateness could lead to being fired. Doing the same task over and over made the day feel very long. Most factory workers labored 10 to 12 hours each day, six days a week. In winter, when it got dark early, oil lamps lit the factory floor. Workers had to squint to see their work. Smoke from the lamps filled the rooms, making people cough.

**In spring, as daylight increased, factories held “blowing-out” celebrations.**  
This marked the end of using oil lamps for the season. These events often included processions and dancing by workers.

**Factories limited freedom in other ways too.**  
Drinking alcohol was not allowed on factory floors. Some factories did not let workers sit down while working. Doors and windows stayed closed, especially in textile mills. This was to stop breezes from messing up delicate fibers. Textile mills often felt unbearably hot and humid in summer. In winter, many workers shivered because the mills were cold. These conditions hurt workers’ health.

**Factories also had serious dangers.**  
Textile factories kept cotton bales near oil used to lubricate machines. This made fires common. Machine accidents happened often. Workers’ hands or fingers could get caught in moving parts and be badly injured or cut off. In severe cases, limbs or entire bodies could be crushed. Anyone who survived such an injury usually lost their job. Without a job, they had no income. Corporal punishment—physical punishment like hitting—was common for both children and adults in factories. In the worst cases, children died from injuries caused by overseers.

**As years passed, conditions in many mills got worse.**  
Workers were given more machines to operate. Owners also increased how fast the machines ran. Wages were often cut. Some workers who once earned an hourly wage now received piecework pay. Piecework meant they were paid only for what they produced, not for the hours they worked. Even piecework pay was sometimes reduced. Low wages plus times with no work made life hard. This was especially true for workers supporting families. For example, in New York City in 1850:  
* The average male factory worker earned about $300 per year.  
* It cost about $600 per year to feed and care for a family of five.

### Work Life Before and During Factories (Dyslexia-Accessible Version - Revised)

**Work before factories was different.**  
Farmers controlled their own work pace. They decided when to do each task. A farmer could fix his fence on Thursday instead of Wednesday if he wanted. Skilled artisans could stop working for the afternoon if they felt like it. Workers often talked together during the day. In some places, journeymen (traveling skilled workers) were promised alcohol as part of their pay. One person might read a book or newspaper aloud to the group. When the weather was warm, doors and windows stayed open. Work stopped when it became too dark to see clearly.

**Work in factories changed a lot.**  
Factory workers had to arrive at a set time. This time was usually very early in the morning. Workers were expected to work all day until their shift ended. They could not leave when they felt tired. Breaks happened only at specific times. If someone arrived late, pay was taken away. Being just 5 minutes late could mean losing several hours of wages. Repeated lateness could lead to being fired. Doing the same task over and over made the day feel very long. Most factory workers labored 10 to 12 hours each day. They worked six days a week. In winter, when it got dark early, oil lamps lit the factory floor. Workers had to squint to see their work. Smoke from the lamps filled the rooms. This made people cough.

**In spring, as daylight increased, factories held “blowing-out” celebrations.**  
This marked the end of using oil lamps for the season. These events often included processions and dancing by workers.

**Factories limited freedom in other ways too.**  
Drinking alcohol was not allowed on factory floors. Some factories did not let workers sit down while working. Doors and windows stayed closed, especially in textile mills. This kept breezes from messing up delicate fibers. Textile mills often felt unbearably hot and humid in summer. In winter, many workers shivered because the mills were cold. These conditions hurt workers’ health.

**Factories also had serious dangers.**  
Textile factories kept cotton bales near oil used to lubricate machines. This made fires common. Machine accidents happened often. Workers’ hands or fingers could get caught in moving parts. They could be badly injured or cut off. In severe cases, limbs or entire bodies could be crushed. Anyone who survived such an injury usually lost their job. Without a job, they had no income. Corporal punishment—physical punishment like hitting—was common for both children and adults in factories. In the worst cases, children died from injuries caused by overseers.

**As years passed, conditions in many mills got worse.**  
Workers were given more machines to operate. Owners also increased how fast the machines ran. Wages were often cut. Some workers who once earned an hourly wage now received piecework pay. Piecework meant they were paid only for what they produced, not for the hours they worked. Even piecework pay was sometimes reduced. Low wages plus times with no work made life hard. This was especially true for workers supporting families. For example, in New York City in 1850:  
* The average male factory worker earned about $300 per year.  
* It cost about $600 per year to feed and care for a family of five.
